'Amuwu: Lands of a Chumash-speaking community on the central California coast, where people built plank canoes called tomol to fish and trade with the Channel Islands.
A'i Cofán/Kofán: The Cofán live in the rainforest along the Ecuador–Colombia border; their language is not related to any neighbouring tongue.
A'uwe: A'uwe is the Xavante people's own name for themselves. They are a Gê-speaking nation of the Mato Grosso savanna in Brazil, known for long-distance log-relay races.
Aaniiih: The Aaniiih (Gros Ventre) are Algonquian-speaking buffalo hunters of the northern Plains, closely related to the Arapaho.
Abbasid Caliphate: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and built Baghdad as their capital in 762. Under Harun al-Rashid it was one of the largest cities in the world.
Abenaki / Abénaquis: The Abenaki are an Algonquian people of northern New England and southern Quebec, and members of the Wabanaki Confederacy.
Abipones: The Abipones were Guaycuruan-speaking hunters of the Gran Chaco. After they adopted the horse they became famous riders.
Abitibiwinni Aki: The homeland of the Abitibiwinni, an Anishinaabe (Algonquin) community around Lake Abitibi in Quebec.
Abnaki: The Abenaki are Algonquian-speaking peoples of Maine, Vermont and New Hampshire, and allies of New France in its wars with English colonists.
Aboriginal Tasmanians: Rising seas cut Tasmania off from mainland Australia about 10,000 years ago, isolating its people for millennia. British colonisation after 1803 devastated them.
Aboriginal tribes: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians had reached the continent at least 50,000 years ago, making theirs among the world's oldest continuous cultures.
Abyssinia: Abyssinia was the old European name for Ethiopia. At Adwa in 1896, Emperor Menelik II crushed an Italian army and kept the country independent.
Acadian Peninsula (UK): This was the old French colony of Acadia, now British Nova Scotia. Britain deported most of the French-speaking Acadians in 1755–1764.
Acaxea: The Acaxee were a farming people of the Sierra Madre Occidental in Durango. They rebelled against Spanish rule in 1601.
Accomack: The Accomac were an Algonquian people of Virginia's Eastern Shore, a tributary of the Powhatan paramount chiefdom.
Accra: Accra was a Ga town on the Gold Coast that grew around Dutch, Danish and English forts. It became the colony's capital in 1877.
Aceh: Aceh was a sultanate at the northern tip of Sumatra that grew rich on pepper. It fought the Dutch from 1873 until about 1904.
Achaemenid Empire: Founded by Cyrus the Great around 550 BC, the empire stretched from Egypt to the Indus, linked by the 2,500 km Royal Road.
Achagua: The Achagua are an Arawakan people of the Colombian and Venezuelan llanos (tropical grasslands).
Achires: The Achires were a small coastal people of Sinaloa in northwest Mexico who lived by fishing.
Acho Dene Koe: The Acho Dene Koe are a Dene people of the upper Liard River, around Fort Liard in Canada's Northwest Territories.
Achuar: The Achuar are a Jivaroan people of the Amazon rainforest on the Ecuador–Peru border.
Achumawi: The Achumawi (Pit River people) lived by fishing, hunting and gathering in the volcanic uplands of northeastern California.
Aché: The Aché are Tupi–Guarani-speaking forest hunters of eastern Paraguay. Some bands lived without settled contact until the 1970s.
Achí: The Achí are a Maya people of the Baja Verapaz highlands in Guatemala, speaking a language close to K'iche'.
Acjachemen (Juaneño): The Acjachemen are the Indigenous people of coastal Orange County, California. Spanish missionaries called them Juaneño after Mission San Juan Capistrano.
Adal: The Adal Sultanate ruled from Harar and Zeila. Under Imam Ahmad Gragn it nearly conquered Ethiopia in the 1530s.
Adena Culture: The Adena were Early Woodland people of the Ohio valley who built burial mounds and earthworks between about 800 BC and AD 100.
Afanasevo: The Afanasievo were Copper Age herders of the Altai and Minusinsk basin, often linked to the ancestors of the Tocharian languages.
Afghanistan: Ahmad Shah Durrani founded the modern Afghan state in 1747. Later it stood as a buffer between the Russian and British empires.
Africa: A small coastal territory near the Niger Delta that the source map labels only "Africa". The delta's trading city-states exported slaves and later palm oil.
Aghlabid Emirate: The Aghlabids governed Ifriqiya (Tunisia) for the Abbasids from 800 to 909. They built the Great Mosque of Kairouan and conquered Sicily.
Agwarmin: The Agwamin are Aboriginal people of the upper Gilbert and Einasleigh rivers in north Queensland.
Ahantchuyuk: The Ahantchuyuk (Pudding River) people were a Kalapuyan band of Oregon's Willamette Valley.
Ahmadnagar: Ahmadnagar was a Deccan sultanate founded in 1490. Its regent Chand Bibi defended it against the Mughals, who annexed it in 1636.
Ahtna Nenn’: The homeland of the Ahtna, a Dene people of Alaska's Copper River basin who traded native copper.
Ahé (Kawahib): The Kawahib are a Tupi–Kawahib people of the Madeira River basin in the Brazilian Amazon.
Aikanã: The Aikanã are a small Indigenous people of Rondônia, Brazil, whose language has no known relatives.
Ainu: The Ainu are the Indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, with their own language and bear-centred religion.
Air: The Sultanate of Aïr, centred on the oasis city of Agadez, controlled Tuareg caravan routes across the Sahara from the 1400s.
Ais: The Ais lived on Florida's Atlantic coast. They rescued and plundered Spanish treasure-fleet shipwrecks.
Akaitcho: The territory of the Yellowknives Dene, named after Akaitcho, a leader who guided John Franklin's 1819–1822 expedition.
Akan: The Akan peoples of the Gold Coast forest built gold-trading states such as Bono and Denkyira. The Asante Empire later grew out of them.
Akatziri: The Akatziri were a nomadic people north of the Black Sea who submitted to Attila's Huns in the 440s.
Akawaio/Akawayo: The Akawaio are a Carib-speaking people of the Pakaraima Mountains of Guyana and Venezuela.
Akimel O'odham (Upper Pima): The Akimel O'odham ("River People") irrigate farms along the Gila River in Arizona, and are probably descendants of the Hohokam.
Akokisa: The Akokisa were an Atakapan people of Galveston Bay on the upper Texas coast.
Akwê: Akwê is the self-name of Gê-speaking peoples of central Brazil, including the Xerente.
Alabama: The Alabama were a Muskogean people of the Alabama River who later joined the Creek Confederacy; the US state is named after them.
Alamans: The Alemanni were a Germanic confederation on the upper Rhine. The French name for Germany, Allemagne, comes from them.
Alans: The Alans were Iranian-speaking nomads of the north Caucasus steppe. Some moved west with the Vandals; others are ancestors of today's Ossetians.
Alawa: The Alawa are Aboriginal people of the Roper River country in Australia's Northern Territory.
Alazapas: The Alazapas were a hunter-gatherer people of Nuevo León in northeastern Mexico.
Albania: Albania declared independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1912. It was ruled by King Zog from 1928 and invaded by Italy in 1939.
Algeria: France invaded Algiers in 1830 and made Algeria part of France itself. Independence came in 1962 after an eight-year war.
Algiers: Algiers was an Ottoman regency ruled by deys, and a base for Barbary corsairs who raided Mediterranean shipping.
Algonquin: The Algonquin are Anishinaabe people of the Ottawa River valley and early fur-trade allies of the French.
Alluvial Lowland Mesolithic Hunter-Forag: Foragers of the Mesopotamian lowlands at the end of the Ice Age, before farming spread down from the surrounding hills.
Almohad Caliphate: A Berber reform movement founded by Ibn Tumart, the Almohads ruled the Maghreb and al-Andalus from about 1147 to 1269.
Almoravid dynasty: The Almoravids were Saharan Berber reformers who founded Marrakesh around 1070 and halted the Christian advance in Spain at Sagrajas in 1086.
Alutiiq (Sugpiaq): The Alutiiq are sea-mammal hunters of Kodiak Island and the Alaska Peninsula who paddled skin-covered kayaks.
Alwa: Alwa was a Christian Nubian kingdom with its capital at Soba, near modern Khartoum. It fell around 1500.
Alyawarre: The Alyawarr are Aboriginal people of the Sandover and Plenty rivers northeast of Alice Springs.
Amahuaca: The Amahuaca are a Panoan people of the forests along the Peru–Brazil border.
Amangu: The Amangu are a Yamatji (Aboriginal) people of the Geraldton coast in Western Australia.
Amarak: The Amurdak are Aboriginal people of the Cobourg Peninsula in western Arnhem Land.
Amazon hunter-gatherers: The Amazon basin was home to many forest peoples. Large earthworks and dark, fertile terra preta soils show that parts of it were also densely farmed.
Ambaló: Ambaló is a small Indigenous community in Cauca, in Colombia's southern Andes.
Amboca: A small Indigenous territory of the Andean foothills in southern Ecuador.
Ambur: Ambur is a town in the Carnatic region of southern India, fought over by the Nawab of Arcot, Mysore and the British.
American Samoa: The eastern Samoan islands became a US territory in 1900. The harbour of Pago Pago was a naval coaling station.
Amorúa: The Amorúa are a Guahibo-speaking people of the Colombian llanos near the Orinoco.
Amuq D: One of the archaeological phases of the Amuq Plain near Antakya, dating to around 5000 BC.
Anambé: The Anambé are a small Tupi–Guarani people of Pará in the Brazilian Amazon.
Anasazi: The Ancestral Puebloans (Anasazi) built cliff dwellings and great houses such as Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon.
Anatolian tribes: Around 2000 BC Anatolia held Hattians, Hurrians and newly arrived Indo-European speakers, the ancestors of the Hittites.
Andean hunter-gatherers: Mobile foragers of the high Andes and the Atacama, who hunted guanaco and vicuña.
Andean states and chiefdoms: After the Wari and Tiwanaku collapsed, the Andes held many regional lordships until the Inca united them in the 1400s.
Andegerebenha: The Andegerebinha are Aboriginal people of the desert country east of Alice Springs.
Andoa: The Andoa were a Zaparoan people of the Pastaza River in the Peruvian Amazon.
Andorra: Andorra is a tiny Pyrenean co-principality, ruled jointly since 1278 by the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix, whose rights later passed to France's head of state.
Andronovo: The Andronovo were Bronze Age herders of the Kazakh steppe, often linked to early Indo-Iranian speakers and the spread of the chariot.
Andyamathanha: The Adnyamathanha ("hills people") live in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia.
Angaité: The Angaité are an Enlhet–Enenlhet people of the Paraguayan Chaco.
Angevin Empire: Henry II of England and his sons ruled England and half of France, from Normandy to Gascony. Most of the French lands were lost in 1204.
Anggamudi: The Anggamudi are Aboriginal people of western Cape York Peninsula, Queensland.
Anglo-Egyptian Sudan: Britain and Egypt formally shared rule of Sudan after the reconquest of 1898, but Britain ran it. Sudan became independent in 1956.
Anglo-Saxons: Germanic Angles, Saxons and Jutes settled eastern Britain in the 400s and 500s after Roman rule ended.
Angola: The Portuguese founded Luanda in 1576 and made it a centre of the Atlantic slave trade. Angola became independent in 1975.
Anguilla: Anguilla is a small Caribbean island, settled by the English in 1650 and still a British overseas territory.
Anguthimri: The Anguthimri are Aboriginal people of the Mapoon area on western Cape York.
Anhalt: Anhalt was a cluster of small German principalities between the Harz mountains and the Elbe.
Anishinabewaki ᐊᓂᔑᓈᐯᐗᑭ: Anishinaabewaki is the homeland of the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi) around the Great Lakes.
Anmatyerre: The Anmatyerr are Aboriginal people of the country north of Alice Springs.
Annam: Annam was the Chinese and French name for central Vietnam. From 1883 it was a French protectorate whose emperors sat at Huế.
Antakarinja: The Antakirinja are Western Desert Aboriginal people of the country around Coober Pedy, South Australia.
Antarctica: No one lived on Antarctica. Several countries had claims, and the 1959 Antarctic Treaty set the continent aside for science.
Antigua and Barbuda: Antigua was an English sugar colony from 1632, worked by enslaved Africans, and a Royal Navy base. It became independent in 1981.
Apache: The Apache are Southern Athabaskan peoples of the Southwest who moved south from Canada centuries before Europeans arrived.
Apalachee: The Apalachee were maize farmers of the Florida panhandle. Spanish missions served them until English-led raids destroyed them in 1704.
Apalachees: The Apalachee were Mississippian maize farmers around Tallahassee, Florida. They fought de Soto's army when it wintered in their capital in 1539â1540.
Aparai: The Aparai are a Carib-speaking people of the Paru River in northern Brazil.
Apiaká: The Apiaká are a Tupi people of the Tapajós and Juruena rivers in Mato Grosso, Brazil.
Apinayé: The Apinajé are a Gê-speaking people of the Tocantins region in Brazil.
Appamattuck: The Appamattuck were a Powhatan-allied Algonquian people of the Appomattox River in Virginia.
Apsaalooké (Crow): The Apsáalooke (Crow) are a Siouan nation of the Yellowstone River country who became renowned horse breeders.
Apyãwa: The Apyãwa (Tapirapé) are a Tupi–Guarani people of Mato Grosso in central Brazil.
Arabana: The Arabana are Aboriginal people of the country around Kati Thanda (Lake Eyre), South Australia.
Arabela: The Arabela are a small Zaparoan people of the Peruvian Amazon.
Arabia: In the late 1800s the Ottomans held the Hejaz and Yemen coasts, while Ha'il's Rashidi emirs and Saudi rivals fought over the interior.
Arabia (Nejd): Ibn Saud captured Riyadh in 1902 and by 1914 ruled Nejd and the eastern province of al-Hasa.
Arabian pastoral nomads: Camels were domesticated in Arabia around the late second millennium BC, which made long desert crossings possible.
Arabs: Arabic-speaking tribes of the Arabian Peninsula, organised in clans that moved between oases and grazing lands.
Aragón: Aragon was a Pyrenean kingdom that united with Catalonia in 1137 and built a Mediterranean empire stretching from Sicily to Naples. It joined Castile when Ferdinand and Isabella married in 1469.
Arakan: Arakan (Rakhine) was a coastal kingdom on the Bay of Bengal, centred on Mrauk U from 1430 until Burma conquered it in 1784.
Arakan (Indian princely state): The Kingdom of Mrauk U in Arakan ruled the Bay of Bengal coast, with Portuguese mercenaries in its service.
Arameans: The Arameans were Semitic-speaking tribes of Syria. Their language, Aramaic, became the common tongue of the Near East.
Araona: The Araona are a small Tacanan people of the Bolivian Amazon.
Arapaho: The Arapaho are Algonquian-speaking people of the central Plains, allied with the Cheyenne.
Arara of Volta Grande: The Arara live at the Volta Grande ("big bend") of the Xingu River in Pará, Brazil.
Arawaks: Arawakan-speaking farmers spread from South America into the Caribbean islands, where they became the ancestors of the Taíno.
Archaic Amerindian hunter-gatherers: Mobile foragers spread across the Americas long before farming. In 2000 BC most of the hemisphere still lived by hunting, fishing and gathering.
Arctic marine mammal hunters: Arctic peoples who hunted seals, walrus and whales, using harpoons, kayaks and snow houses.
Argentina: Argentina declared independence from Spain in 1816. After 1880 it drew millions of European immigrants and became a major grain and beef exporter.
Arikapú: The Arikapú are a tiny Macro-Jê people of Rondônia, Brazil, whose language has very few speakers.
Arikara: The Arikara were Caddoan-speaking farmers of the Missouri River who lived in earth-lodge villages.
Arma: The Arma were descendants of the Moroccan soldiers who conquered Songhai in 1591, and ruled Timbuktu as pashas.
Armenia: Armenia, in the highlands around Mount Ararat, became the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion, in about 301.
Armorica: Armorica was the Roman name for Brittany. Britons fleeing the Anglo-Saxons settled here in the 400s and 500s.
Arosaguntacook: The Arosaguntacook were an Abenaki people of the Androscoggin River in Maine.
Arran: Arran (Caucasian Albania) was a lowland region of today's Azerbaijan, ruled by local dynasties under Islamic overlords.
Arrernte: The Arrernte are Aboriginal people of the country around Mparntwe (Alice Springs) in central Australia.
Arrohatec: The Arrohattoc were a Powhatan chiefdom on the James River in Virginia, near today's Richmond.
Artsakh: Artsakh was an Armenian principality in the mountains of Karabakh.
Aruá: The Aruá are a small Tupi people of Rondônia in Brazil.
Asante: The Asante Empire was founded around 1701 around the Golden Stool. It controlled the Gold Coast's gold and slave trade until British conquest.
Aseniwuche Winewak (Rocky Mountain): The Aseniwuche Winewak ("Rocky Mountain People") are Cree and Haudenosaunee descendants from the Grande Cache area of Alberta.
Ashaninka: The Asháninka are one of the largest Amazonian peoples, living in the central forests of Peru.
Asheninka: The Ashéninka, close kin of the Asháninka, live in the Gran Pajonal and nearby river valleys of Peru.
Ashikaga shogunate: The Ashikaga shoguns ruled Japan from Kyoto from 1336. Their power collapsed in the Ōnin War of 1467–1477.
Assam: The Ahom kings ruled the Brahmaputra valley for six centuries and beat back Mughal invasions. Britain annexed Assam in 1826.
Assiniboin: The Assiniboine are a Siouan people of the northern Plains who allied with the Cree in the fur trade.
Assiniboine: The Assiniboine (Nakota) were buffalo hunters of the Saskatchewan and Missouri prairies, closely related to the Sioux.
Assyria: Assyria was based in the northern Tigris cities of Ashur and Nineveh. It built the largest empire the world had yet seen before falling in 612 BC.
Astrakhan Khanate: The Khanate of Astrakhan was a Tatar successor of the Golden Horde at the mouth of the Volga. Ivan the Terrible conquered it in 1556.
Asturias: Asturias was a small Christian kingdom in the northern mountains of Spain, founded after the victory at Covadonga in about 722.
Atakapa: The Atakapa were coastal fishers and hunters of southwest Louisiana and east Texas.
Atakapa Ishak Chawasha: A present-day tribal nation of the Louisiana coast, made up of Atakapa-Ishak and Chawasha descendants.
Atakapa-Ishak: The Atakapa-Ishak lived along the Gulf coast of Louisiana and Texas. Their language has no close relatives.
Atfalati: The Atfalati (Tualatin) were a Kalapuyan people of the Tualatin Valley, west of today's Portland, Oregon.
Athabaskan: Athabaskan-speaking Dene peoples spread across the boreal forest of Alaska and northwest Canada.
Atikum-Umã: The Atikum are an Indigenous community of the dry sertão of Pernambuco in northeast Brazil.
Ato trading confederacy: A palm-oil trading community of the Niger Delta region, drawn into British control in the 1880s and 1890s.
Atropatene: Atropatene was a kingdom in today's Iranian Azerbaijan, founded by the Persian satrap Atropates after Alexander's conquest. The region's name comes from his.
Atsugewi: The Atsugewi (Hat Creek people) lived in northeastern California and spoke a language related to Achumawi.
Attiwonderonk (Neutral): The Neutral Confederacy were Iroquoian farmers of the Niagara peninsula. The French called them "neutral" because they stayed out of Huron–Iroquois wars.
Aucocisco: The Aucocisco were an Abenaki people of Casco Bay, near today's Portland, Maine.
Aures: The Aurès mountains of Algeria were a Berber stronghold where Queen Dihya (Kahina) resisted the Arab conquest around 700.
Australia: The six British colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901.
Australian aboriginal hunter-gatherers: Hundreds of Aboriginal nations, speaking about 250 languages, managed the continent with fire and seasonal movement.
Austria: The Republic of Austria was the German-speaking core of the Habsburg Empire after 1918. It was annexed by Germany in 1938 and restored in 1945.
Austria-Hungary: The Compromise of 1867 split the Habsburg Empire into two states sharing one emperor. It broke apart at the end of World War I in 1918.
Austrian Empire: Francis II proclaimed the Austrian Empire in 1804 as the Holy Roman Empire neared its end. It became Austria-Hungary in 1867.
Austrian Netherlands: The southern Netherlands, roughly today's Belgium, passed from Spain to Austria in 1714. France annexed them in 1795.
Austro-Asiatic rice cultures: Early rice farmers of mainland Southeast Asia, probably speakers of Austroasiatic languages, ancestors of Mon and Khmer.
Austronesians: Austronesian seafarers spread from Taiwan through the Philippines and Indonesia, and later across the Pacific and Indian oceans to Madagascar.
Ava: The Kingdom of Ava, named after its capital on the Irrawaddy, was the main power of Upper Burma from 1364 to 1555. The Toungoo kings later ruled from there too.
Avanti: Avanti was one of the sixteen great kingdoms (mahajanapadas) of ancient India, with its capital at Ujjain.
Avars: The Avars were steppe nomads who ruled the Carpathian Basin from the 560s and besieged Constantinople in 626. Charlemagne destroyed their khaganate in the 790s.
Awabakal: The Awabakal are Aboriginal people of Lake Macquarie and Newcastle, New South Wales.
Awaeté: The Asurini of the Xingu (Awaeté) are a Tupi–Guarani people of Pará, Brazil.
Awaeté (Asurini of the Xingu): The Asurini of the Xingu are a Tupi–Guarani people known for elaborate geometric body painting.
Awajún: The Awajún (Aguaruna) are a Jivaroan people of the upper Marañón River in northern Peru.
Awaswas: The Awaswas were an Ohlone people of the Santa Cruz coast in California.
Awngthim: The Awngthim are Aboriginal people of the Weipa area on western Cape York.
Awsa: The Imamate of Aussa was an Afar sultanate in the Awash River valley of today's Ethiopia.
Awytyza: A small Indigenous territory in Mato Grosso, central Brazil.
Awá: The Awá (Guajá) are among the last hunter-gatherers of the eastern Amazon, in Maranhão.
Axum: The Kingdom of Aksum traded Red Sea ivory and gold, minted its own coins, and adopted Christianity in the 300s.
Ayahuacas: A small Andean community in the highlands of northern Peru.
Aymara: The Aymara live around Lake Titicaca. The Inca absorbed their kingdoms in the 1400s.
Aymara kingdoms: Aymara lordships such as the Lupaca and Colla ruled the Titicaca basin before the Inca conquest.
Ayoreo: The Ayoreo are Zamucoan-speaking forest people of the northern Chaco in Bolivia and Paraguay.
Ayutthaya: Siam's capital from 1351 to 1767, Ayutthaya was a cosmopolitan trading city and one of the largest in Asia. Burmese armies sacked it in 1767.
Ayuukjä'äy (Mixe): The Ayuuk (Mixe) people of the Oaxaca highlands successfully resisted both the Aztecs and the Spanish.
Ayyubid Sultanate: Saladin founded the Ayyubid dynasty, ended the Fatimid Caliphate, and retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.
Azandes: The Azande are a central African people of today's South Sudan, Congo and Central African Republic.
Azerbaijan: The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic of 1918 is often called the first democratic republic in the Muslim world. Baku's oil fields made it one of the world's great oil centres around 1900.
Aztec Empire: The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan ruled central Mexico from 1428. Tenochtitlan was larger than any city in Spain.
Añuu: The Añú are a lake-dwelling people of Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela. Their houses on stilts inspired the name "Venezuela" ("little Venice").
Aónikenk (Tehuelche): The Aónikenk (southern Tehuelche) were guanaco hunters of the Patagonian steppe, and among the tallest people Europeans had seen.
Babylonia: Babylonia was the land of southern Mesopotamia, with Babylon as its capital. Hammurabi issued his law code there around 1754 BC.
Bactria: Bactria lay between the Hindu Kush and the Oxus river (Amu Darya). Alexander's successors ruled it as a Greco-Bactrian kingdom in the 200s BC.
Baden: Baden was a southwestern German state on the Rhine. Napoleon raised it to a grand duchy in 1806.
Badimaya: The Badimia are Aboriginal people of the Mount Magnet area in Western Australia's mid-west.
Badtjala: The Butchulla are Aboriginal people of K'gari (Fraser Island) and the nearby Queensland coast.
Bagirmi: Bagirmi was a sultanate southeast of Lake Chad, founded around 1522. It paid tribute to Bornu and Wadai.
Bahamas: The Bahamas is where Columbus first landed in 1492. The islands became a British colony and gained independence in 1973.
Bahawalpur: Bahawalpur was a princely state on the Sutlej River ruled by Daudpotra nawabs from 1748. It joined Pakistan in 1947.
Bahmani Kingdom: The Bahmani Sultanate ruled the Deccan from 1347. By 1500 it had shrunk to the area around Bidar, as five successor sultanates broke away.
Bakanh: The Pakanh are Aboriginal people of central Cape York Peninsula.
Balhae: Balhae was founded in 698 by Dae Joyeong, a former Goguryeo general, and ruled Manchuria and northern Korea until the Khitans destroyed it in 926.
Ballardong: The Ballardong are a Noongar people of the Avon Valley around York, Western Australia.
Baltic tribes: Baltic-speaking peoples (Prussians, Lithuanians, Latvians) lived along the southeast Baltic and were among Europe's last pagans.
Balts: Speakers of Baltic languages, among the oldest-surviving branches of Indo-European.
Banas: The Banas were a dynasty of eastern Deccan chiefs who served the Pallavas and Chalukyas as vassals.
Banawá: The Banawá are a small Arawan people of the Purus River basin in Amazonas, Brazil.
Bandjigali: The Bandjigali are Aboriginal people of the Broken Hill area in far western New South Wales.
Banggarla: The Barngarla are Aboriginal people of Eyre Peninsula, South Australia.
Bangladesh: East Bengal became East Pakistan in 1947, then won independence as Bangladesh in the 1971 Liberation War.
Banjima: The Banyjima are Aboriginal people of the Hamersley Range in the Pilbara, Western Australia.
Bantu: Around 2000 BC, Bantu-speaking farmers began moving out of the Nigeria–Cameroon borderlands, eventually spreading across most of sub-Saharan Africa.
Bantu peoples: Bantu-speaking farmers and ironworkers had settled most of central, eastern and southern Africa by AD 500.
Baraba Baraba: The Baraba Baraba are Aboriginal people of the Murray River near Swan Hill, Victoria.
Baradha: The Barada are Aboriginal people of central Queensland.
Barasano/Panenoá: The Barasana are Tukanoan people of the Vaupés region of Colombia, known for marrying across language groups.
Barbados: Barbados was an English colony from 1627 and the first great sugar island of the Caribbean, built on enslaved labour. It became independent in 1966.
Barbados (UK): Barbados was an English sugar island worked by enslaved Africans, and one of Britain's richest colonies in the 1700s.
Bardi: The Bardi are saltwater people of the Dampier Peninsula in the Kimberley, Western Australia.
Barghawata: The Barghawata were a Berber confederacy of Morocco's Atlantic coast that followed its own prophet and its own Quran from the 740s to about 1058.
Barindji: The Barindji are Aboriginal people of the lower Darling River in New South Wales.
Barkindji: The Barkindji ("river people") live along the Darling River (Baaka) in New South Wales.
Barna: The Barna are Aboriginal people of central Queensland.
Barotse: Barotseland was the Lozi kingdom of the upper Zambezi floodplain, which became a British protectorate in 1900.
Barranbinya: The Barranbinya are Aboriginal people of the Bourke area on the Darling River, New South Wales.
Barundji: The Barundji are Aboriginal people of western New South Wales.
Barunggam: The Barunggam are Aboriginal people of the Darling Downs in southeast Queensland.
Baré: The Baré are an Arawakan people of the upper Rio Negro in Brazil and Venezuela.
Barí: The Barí are a Chibchan people of the Catatumbo forests on the Colombia–Venezuela border.
Bashkirs: The Bashkirs are a Turkic people of the southern Ural Mountains.
Basques: The Basques of the western Pyrenees speak a language unrelated to any other living language, older than the Indo-European tongues of Europe.
Basutoland: Basutoland was the mountain kingdom of King Moshoeshoe, who sought British protection in 1868 to escape Boer expansion. It became independent as Lesotho in 1966.
Batavian Republic: The Batavian Republic was the French-backed successor to the Dutch Republic, set up in 1795.
Batsil Winik' Otik (Tzotzil): The Tzotzil are a Maya people of the Chiapas highlands around San Cristóbal de las Casas.
Baure: The Baure are an Arawakan people of the Llanos de Moxos in Bolivia, a region of ancient raised fields and causeways.
Bavaria: Bavaria was a duchy, then an electorate, in southern Germany. Napoleon made it a kingdom in 1806.
Bavarii: The Baiuvarii were a Germanic people who settled the land between the Danube and the Alps in the 500s and gave Bavaria its name.
Bay of Honduras settlements: The settlements were the base of British logwood cutters, the origin of today's Belize.
Bayali: The Bayali are Aboriginal people of the Gladstone area in Queensland.
Beaker: The Beaker culture is named after its bell-shaped drinking cups. It spread across western Europe around 2500–2000 BC, along with copper working.
Beaver: The Dane-zaa (Beaver) are Dene people of the Peace River country in Canada.
Beaver Lake Cree: The Beaver Lake Cree are a Cree Nation of northeastern Alberta.
Bechuanaland Protectorate: Bechuanaland was a British protectorate requested by Tswana chiefs to block Boer and Rhodes expansion. It became independent as Botswana in 1966.
Bedouins: The Bedouin were Arab camel-herding nomads who carried Islam and Arabic into the Sahara.
Bega: The Beja are Cushitic-speaking nomads of the Red Sea hills, the Blemmyes of classical writers.
Beja people: The Beja are Cushitic-speaking camel herders of the hills between the Nile and the Red Sea.
Belarus: Belarus became independent from the USSR in 1991. Its name means "White Rus'".
Belgian Congo: Belgium took over King Leopold II's Congo Free State in 1908 after international outrage at forced-labour atrocities. It became independent in 1960.
Belgium: Belgium broke away from the Netherlands in 1830. It was invaded by Germany in both world wars.
Belize: Belize was formerly British Honduras. It became independent in 1981, while Guatemala still claimed it.
Bell-shaped burials culture: An Iron Age culture of the Vistula basin in Poland, named after its burials under bell-shaped clay vessels.
Bella: A coastal people of northern British Columbia, where cedar-plank villages lived on salmon and sea mammals.
Ben 'Zaa/Binnizá/Mén Diiste/Bene Xhon (Z: The Zapotec of Oaxaca built Monte Albán, one of Mesoamerica's first cities, around 500 BC.
Bengal: Bengal was a rich delta sultanate and then a Mughal province. Victory at Plassey in 1757 gave the East India Company control here.
Bengal Presidency: The East India Company's Bengal Presidency was ruled from Calcutta, the capital of British India until 1911.
Benin: Dahomey became independent from France in 1960 and was renamed Benin in 1975.
Beothuk: The Beothuk were the people of Newfoundland, possibly the "Red Indians" of early accounts, after their red-ochre body paint. The last known Beothuk, Shanawdithit, died in 1829.
Berar: Berar was one of five Deccan sultanates that broke from the Bahmanis in 1490. Ahmadnagar absorbed it in 1574.
Berber Tribes: Berber (Amazigh) tribes of the western Sahara controlled caravan routes between Morocco and the Sahel.
Berbers: The Amazigh (Berbers) are the Indigenous peoples of North Africa, from Morocco to the Siwa oasis.
Betoy: The Betoy were a people of the Colombian llanos, now largely absorbed into other groups.
Beylik of Aydin: The Aydinids were a Turkish emirate on Anatolia's Aegean coast whose fleets raided the Aegean. The Ottomans annexed it in 1426.
Bhutan: Bhutan was unified in the 1600s by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, a Tibetan lama. It became a monarchy in 1907.
Bia Mbyá: A Guarani community territory in eastern Bolivia.
Bibbulman: The Bibbulmun are Noongar people of the far southwest of Western Australia.
Bidai: The Bidai were a Caddoan-influenced people of the Trinity River in east Texas.
Bidar: Bidar was the last Bahmani capital, which became the Barid Shahi sultanate. Bijapur annexed it in 1619.
Bidjara: The Bidjara are Aboriginal people of the Carnarvon Ranges in central Queensland.
Bidwell: The Bidawal are Aboriginal people of the forested ranges of East Gippsland, Victoria.
Big Stone Cree: The Big Stone Cree are a Woodland Cree nation of northern Alberta.
Bigambul: The Bigambul are Aboriginal people of the Queensland–New South Wales border country.
Bijapur: The Adil Shahi sultanate of Bijapur built the Gol Gumbaz, one of the world's largest domes. The Mughals conquered it in 1686.
Bilinara: The Bilinarra are Aboriginal people of the Victoria River district, Northern Territory.
Biloxi: The Biloxi were a Siouan-speaking people of the Mississippi Gulf coast; the city is named after them.
Binbinga: The Binbinga are Aboriginal people of the McArthur River country, Northern Territory.
Bindjali: The Bindjali are Aboriginal people of the Wimmera, western Victoria.
Biri: The Biri are Aboriginal people of the Bowen River region of central Queensland.
Biripi: The Biripi are Aboriginal people of the Manning River on the mid-north coast of New South Wales.
Birria: The Birria are Aboriginal people of central western Queensland.
Bithynia: Bithynia was a Hellenistic kingdom on the Asian shore of the Bosporus. Its last king left it to Rome in 74 BC.
Blackfoot: The Blackfoot Confederacy (Siksika, Kainai and Piikani) dominated the northwestern Plains with horse and gun in the 1700s.
Blemmyes: The Blemmyes were nomads of the eastern desert between the Nile and the Red Sea. They raided Roman Egypt.
Blue Horde: The Blue Horde was the western wing of the Golden Horde, whose khans ruled from Sarai on the lower Volga.
Bodéwadmiakiwen (Potawatomi): The Potawatomi ("keepers of the fire") are an Anishinaabe people of the southern Great Lakes.
Boe: Boe is the self-name of the Bororo, a Gê-speaking people of Mato Grosso known for circular villages.
Bohanes: The Bohanes were a Charrúan people of the Uruguay River.
Boihaenum: Boiohaemum, "home of the Boii", was the old name for Bohemia, held by the Germanic Marcomanni in Roman times.
Boii: The Boii were a Celtic people of the Po valley and Bohemia. Bohemia is named after them.
Bolivia: Bolivia is named after Simón Bolívar and became independent in 1825. It lost its coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884).
Boonwurrung: The Boonwurrung are Kulin people of the Port Phillip Bay coast around Melbourne.
Bora: The Bora are a Witotoan people of the Peru–Colombia Amazon border, known for their drum language.
Borgu States: Borgu was a group of Bariba kingdoms, including Nikki and Bussa, divided between French Dahomey and British Nigeria in 1898.
Boriken Taino: Boriken is the Taíno name for Puerto Rico, home to chiefdoms that the Spanish conquered after 1508.
Bosnia: The medieval Kingdom of Bosnia reached its height under King Tvrtko I (1377–1391). The Ottomans conquered it in 1463.
Bosnia and Herzegovina: Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1992, which was followed by a war that lasted until 1995.
Bosnia-Herzegovina: Austria-Hungary occupied the Ottoman province in 1878 and annexed it in 1908. It was where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was killed in 1914.
Bosporan Kingdom: The Bosporan Kingdom was a Greek kingdom on the Kerch Strait in Crimea that sold Black Sea grain to Athens.
Bosporian Kingdom: The Bosporan Kingdom was a Roman client kingdom on the Kerch Strait, ruled by Hellenised kings until the 300s AD.
Bostos: A small Indigenous territory in Central America.
Botswana: Botswana became independent in 1966. Diamonds discovered soon after made it one of Africa's fastest-growing economies.
Brandenburg: The Margraviate of Brandenburg, centred on Berlin, was the core of the Hohenzollern lands that became Prussia.
Brazil: Brazil declared independence from Portugal in 1822 as an empire under Pedro I. It became a republic in 1889.
Bremen: Bremen is a Hanseatic city-state on the Weser River, a free imperial city since 1646.
Bribri: The Bribri are a Chibchan people of the Talamanca mountains in Costa Rica.
British American colonies: These were the thirteen British colonies on the Atlantic seaboard of North America, which declared independence in 1776.
British Central Africa Protectorate: Britain's protectorate around Lake Malawi, founded in 1891, was renamed Nyasaland in 1907.
British East Africa: The East Africa Protectorate (Kenya) was built around the Uganda Railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria.
British East India Company: The Company was a chartered trading company with its own army. By 1815 it ruled much of India as a sovereign power.
British Guiana: British Guiana was a sugar colony on South America's north coast, worked by enslaved Africans and later by indentured Indians. It became independent as Guyana in 1966.
British Honduras: British Honduras was a colony on the Caribbean coast of Central America, built on logwood and mahogany. It became independent as Belize in 1981.
British India: In 1945 British India was nearing its end. Independence and partition came in August 1947, with about 15 million people displaced.
British Malaya: British Malaya was a patchwork of Straits Settlements and protected Malay sultanates, rich in tin and rubber.
British North America: These were Britain's remaining colonies north of the United States after 1783, which united as Canada in 1867.
British Protectorate: These were British-protected sheikhdoms and sultanates along the southern and eastern coasts of Arabia.
British Raj: After the 1857 uprising, the British Crown ruled India directly from 1858 to 1947, alongside about 560 princely states.
British Somaliland: British Somaliland was a protectorate on the Gulf of Aden, valued for supplying meat to Aden. It joined Somalia in 1960.
Brittany: Brittany was a Celtic duchy in northwest France, independent until it was united with the French crown in 1532.
Broërec: Bro Waroch was a Breton kingdom around Vannes, named after its 500s ruler Waroch.
Brunei: Brunei was a once-powerful Bornean sultanate that lost most of its land to Sarawak's White Rajahs. It became a British protectorate in 1888.
Brunka: The Brunka (Boruca) are a Chibchan people of southern Costa Rica, known for their carved masks.
Brunswick: Brunswick was a German duchy ruled by a branch of the Welf (Guelph) dynasty.
Brushed Pottery culture: An Iron Age culture of the eastern Baltic, linked to early Baltic-speaking peoples.
Buandig: The Bunganditj are Aboriginal people of the Mount Gambier area in South Australia.
Budjari: The Budjari are Aboriginal people of southwestern Queensland.
Buganda: Buganda is a kingdom on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, ruled by a kabaka. It was the core of Britain's Uganda Protectorate.
Buglé and Ngäbé: The Ngäbe and Buglé are Chibchan peoples of western Panama's mountains.
Bukhara Khanate: Bukhara was a Silk Road oasis state ruled by Uzbek khans and later emirs, and a Russian protectorate from 1868.
Bukurnidja: The Bukurnidja are Aboriginal people of Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory.
Bularnu: The Bularnu are Aboriginal people of the Georgina River region in northwest Queensland.
Bulgaria: Bulgaria became autonomous from the Ottomans in 1878 and fully independent in 1908.
Bulgars: The Bulgars were Turkic nomads of the Pontic steppe. One group founded Bulgaria on the Danube in 681; another founded Volga Bulgaria.
Bundelkhand: Bundelkhand is a hilly region of central India ruled by Bundela Rajput chiefs, many of whom became British allies around 1800.
Bundjalung: The Bundjalung are Aboriginal people of the far north coast of New South Wales.
Bunyoro: Bunyoro-Kitara is a kingdom of western Uganda. King Kabalega resisted British conquest until 1899.
Burarra: The Burarra are Aboriginal people of the Maningrida area in Arnhem Land.
Burgundians: The Burgundians were an East Germanic people who settled the Rhône valley in the 400s and gave Burgundy its name.
Burgundy: Burgundy was a duchy in eastern France whose Valois dukes in the 1400s ruled a rich realm stretching to the Low Countries.
Burkina Faso: Burkina Faso, "land of upright people", was formerly Upper Volta. Thomas Sankara renamed it in 1984.
Burma: Burma's Konbaung kings fought three wars with Britain, which annexed the whole country by 1885. It became independent in 1948.
Burmese: Tibeto-Burman-speaking peoples moving south from the eastern Himalaya, ancestors of the Burmese and Pyu.
Burmese kingdoms: In the 1500s the Toungoo dynasty reunited Burma and briefly built the largest empire in Southeast Asian history.
Burundi: Burundi is an old kingdom of the Great Lakes highlands, ruled by Germany and then Belgium before independence in 1962.
Buyid Emirates: The Buyids were a Shia Daylamite dynasty from the Caspian highlands who took Baghdad in 945 and ruled Iraq and western Iran.
Byelorussian SSR: The Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic was declared in 1919–1920 and became a founding member of the USSR in 1922.
Byzantine Empire: The Byzantine Empire was the eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople. It lasted until the Ottomans took the city in 1453.
Bïde: A small Indigenous territory in the Brazilian Amazon.
Cabiyari/Kawiyarí: The Kawiyarí are a small Arawakan people of the Apaporis River in Colombia.
Caddo: The Caddo were mound-building farmers of the Red River region. "Texas" comes from their word taysha, "friend".
Cahita: The Cahita peoples, including the Yaqui and Mayo, lived along the rivers of Sonora and Sinaloa in Mexico.
Cahitas: The Cahita-speaking Yaqui and Mayo of northwest Mexico. The Yaqui resisted Spanish and Mexican rule for centuries.
Cahto: The Cahto are a small Athabaskan people of the Mendocino coast range in California.
Cahuilla: The Cahuilla are desert people of inland southern California who lived near palm oases and springs.
Cahulia: The Cahuilla lived in the Coachella Valley and nearby mountains of southern California.
Calabar: Calabar was an Efik trading town on the Cross River and a major port for slaves, then for palm oil.
Caldwell: The Caldwell First Nation is an Anishinaabe community of the Lake Erie shore near Point Pelee, Ontario.
Calicuas: A small Indigenous territory in the Appalachian region.
Caliphate of Córdoba: Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph in 929. His capital Córdoba was then western Europe's largest city.
Caloosahatchee culture: The Caloosahatchee culture was the ancient fishing culture of southwest Florida, ancestral to the Calusa.
Calusa: The Calusa of southwest Florida built a powerful kingdom without farming, living on the estuaries' fish and shellfish.
Calvas: A small Andean community in southern Ecuador.
Cambodia: Cambodia is the heir of the Khmer Empire, squeezed between Siam and Vietnam until it became a French protectorate in 1863.
Cameroon: French and British Cameroons were united as Cameroon on independence in 1960–1961.
Canaan: Canaan was the land of Semitic city-states along the Levant coast, where the alphabet was invented.
Canaanite city-states: Canaan's city-states, such as Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer, came under Egyptian control after about 1550 BC.
Canada: The Dominion of Canada was formed in 1867 and stretched from sea to sea once Rupert's Land (1870) and British Columbia (1871) joined.
Canary Islands: The Canary Islands were Spain's Atlantic stepping stone, where Columbus and the treasure fleets stopped on the way to the Americas.
Canela Apanyekrá: The Apanyekrá Canela are a Timbira (Gê) people of Maranhão, Brazil.
Canela Ramkokamekrá: The Ramkokamekrá Canela are a Timbira people of Maranhão known for log-relay races.
Canichana: The Canichana are a small people of the Bolivian Moxos plains.
Cantia: Cantia was the Roman-era name for Kent, which became the Anglo-Saxon Kingdom of Kent.
Cape Colony: The Dutch East India Company founded Cape Town in 1652 as a supply station. Britain took the colony in 1795 and kept it from 1806.
Cape Fear: The Cape Fear Indians were a small Siouan people at the mouth of the Cape Fear River in North Carolina.
Cappadocia: Cappadocia was a kingdom in central Anatolia, ruled by an Iranian dynasty after Alexander.
Carcross/Tagish First Nation (BC): The Carcross/Tagish are Tagish and Tlingit people of the Yukon–British Columbia border lakes.
Carcross/Tagish First Nation (Yukon): The Carcross/Tagish are a First Nation of the Yukon's Southern Lakes. Their members helped spark the 1896 Klondike gold rush.
Caribbean hunter-gatherers: The first islanders reached the Caribbean from South and Central America by canoe, about 6,000 years ago.
Carnatic: The Carnatic was the Coromandel coast under the Nawabs of Arcot, the battlefield of the Anglo-French wars in India.
Carolingian Empire: Charlemagne was crowned emperor in Rome on Christmas Day 800, reviving the idea of a western empire.
Carthage: After losing the Second Punic War in 201 BC, Carthage kept only its African hinterland. Rome destroyed it in 146 BC.
Carthaginian Empire: Carthage, a Phoenician colony in Tunisia, built a trading empire across the western Mediterranean.
Cascades: The Cascades (Watlala) were Chinookan people of the Columbia River Gorge.
Castile: Castile was the largest Christian kingdom of medieval Spain, which led the Reconquista and united with Aragon in 1479.
Catacomb culture: The Catacomb culture was a Bronze Age steppe culture north of the Black Sea, named after its side-chamber burials.
Catawba: The Catawba are a Siouan people of the Carolina Piedmont, known for their pottery.
Caucasian Alans: The Alans of the north Caucasus were Iranian-speaking horse peoples and ancestors of the Ossetians.
Caucasian Albania: Caucasian Albania was an ancient Christian kingdom in today's Azerbaijan, unrelated to Balkan Albania.
Caxas: A small Andean community in the highlands of northern Peru.
Caxcan: The Caxcan were a Nahuatl-speaking people of Zacatecas and Jalisco who led the Mixtón War against Spain (1540–1542).
Caxcane: The Caxcan of western Mexico rose against Spanish rule in the Mixtón War of 1540–1542.
Cayenne: Cayenne was the French colony on the Guiana coast, later known for its penal colony on Devil's Island.
Cayubaba: The Cayubaba are a small people of the Bolivian Moxos plains.
Cayuse: The Cayuse of the Columbia Plateau were famous horse breeders; "cayuse" became the word for a pony.
Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla: The Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla were Plateau peoples of the Columbia River in Oregon and Washington.
Celtiberians: The Celtiberians were Celtic-speaking peoples of central Spain who held out against Rome until Numantia fell in 133 BC.
Celtic kingdoms: These were the Irish and Welsh kingdoms beyond Anglo-Saxon and Norman control.
Celts: The Celtic-speaking peoples of the Iron Age spread across Europe, from Ireland to Anatolia.
Central African Republic: Ubangi-Shari became independent from France in 1960 as the Central African Republic.
Central Andean chiefdoms: After Wari collapsed, the central Andes split into regional chiefdoms until the Inca conquest.
Central Andean peoples: Andean peoples of the central highlands such as the Huanca, who were part of the Inca Empire in 1492.
Central Pomo: The Central Pomo are a Pomoan people of the Russian River in California, renowned basket-makers.
Ceylon: Ceylon is the island now called Sri Lanka. The Portuguese and then the Dutch held its coasts, while the kingdom of Kandy held the interior until Britain took it in 1815.
Ceylon (Dutch): The Dutch East India Company took Ceylon's coasts from Portugal between 1638 and 1658 for its cinnamon. Britain seized them in 1796.
Ch'orti': The Ch'orti' are a Maya people of eastern Guatemala and western Honduras, near the ancient city of Copán.
Chachi: The Chachi are a Barbacoan people of the rainforest rivers of Esmeraldas, Ecuador.
Chad: Chad was the northern end of French Equatorial Africa and became independent in 1960. Lake Chad lies at its western edge.
Chafan: A small Kalapuyan band of Oregon's Willamette Valley.
Chagatai Khanate: The Chagatai Khanate was the Central Asian share of Genghis Khan's empire, given to his second son Chagatai.
Chahta Yakni (Choctaw): Chahta Yakni is the homeland of the Choctaw, a Muskogean nation of central Mississippi.
ChalAt’i’lo t’sikAti (Chalat’): The Chalat' (Hoh) are a Quileute-related people of the Hoh River on Washington's Olympic coast.
Chalon: The Chalon were an Ohlone (Costanoan) people of the Salinas valley in California.
Chalukya Empire: The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani ruled the western Deccan from 973 to 1189 and fought the Cholas.
Chalukyas: The Chalukyas of Badami ruled the Deccan from 543 to 753. Pulakeshin II defeated Emperor Harsha around 618.
Chamicuro: The Chamicuro are a small Arawakan people of the Huallaga river in Peru, whose language is almost extinct.
Champa: Champa was a group of Cham kingdoms on the central Vietnamese coast, built on maritime trade. Hindu temples such as My Son survive.
Champa City States: Cham city-states such as Vijaya and Panduranga, which shared the coast after Khmer and Vietnamese wars.
Champagne & Aishihik: The Champagne and Aishihik First Nations are Southern Tutchone people of the southwest Yukon.
Chandellas: The Chandela Rajputs of Bundelkhand built the temples of Khajuraho in the 900s and 1000s.
Chango: The Chango were fishing peoples of the Atacama Desert coast who hunted sea lions from inflated sealskin rafts.
Chankas: The Chanka confederation of the central Andes nearly destroyed Cusco around 1438. Their defeat launched the Inca Empire's rise.
Chaná: The Chaná were a people of the Paraná delta and the lower Uruguay River.
Chané: The Chané were Arawakan farmers of the Andean foothills of Bolivia and Argentina, later absorbed by the Guarani.
Chaparra: A small Andean community territory in southern Ecuador.
Chapra: The Chapra are a Candoshi-speaking people of the Peruvian Amazon.
Charka: The Charka were an Andean people of central Bolivia, part of the Charcas confederation.
Charrúa: The Charrúa were nomadic hunters of Uruguay and Entre Ríos who resisted Spanish settlement for three centuries.
Chatot: The Chatot were a people of the Apalachicola River in the Florida panhandle, served by Spanish missions in the 1600s.
Chauhans: The Chahamanas (Chauhans) of Sambhar and Ajmer were a Rajput dynasty. Prithviraj III fought Muhammad of Ghor in 1191–1192.
Chavin: The Chavín culture is named after the temple at Chavín de Huántar in Peru's highlands. It spread a shared religious art across the Andes.
Chehalis: The Chehalis are a Salish people of southwest Washington's Chehalis River.
Chelamela: The Chelamela were a Kalapuyan band of the upper Willamette Valley in Oregon.
Chelan: The Chelan are a Salish people of Lake Chelan in Washington.
Chelmia: A small South Slavic principality on the Adriatic coast, in the Montenegro region.
Chemapho: A small Kalapuyan band of the Willamette Valley, Oregon.
Chenla: Chenla was the Khmer kingdom that absorbed Funan in the 500s and 600s. It was the forerunner of Angkor.
Chepenefa: The Chepenefa (Mary's River) were a Kalapuyan band near today's Corvallis, Oregon.
Cheras: The Cheras ruled the Malabar coast of Kerala. They were one of the three crowned dynasties of ancient Tamil poetry, with the Cholas and Pandyas.
Cheraw: The Cheraw were a Siouan people of the Carolina Piedmont.
Chernoles culture: The Chernoles culture was an Iron Age farming culture of the forest-steppe in Ukraine, sometimes linked to early Slavs.
Cheroenhaka (Nottoway): The Cheroenhaka (Nottoway) are an Iroquoian people of southeastern Virginia.
Cherokee: The Cherokee are an Iroquoian nation of the southern Appalachians. In 1838 the US forcibly removed them west on the Trail of Tears.
Cherokee (Oklahoma): Present-day reservation lands of the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma, where they were forced to move in 1838–1839.
Chesapeake: The Chesepian were an Algonquian people of southeastern Virginia; the bay is named after them.
Cheyenne: The Cheyenne were Algonquian farmers who moved onto the Plains and became horse-mounted bison hunters.
Cheyenne-Arapaho (Oklahoma): The Oklahoma reservation lands assigned to the Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho in 1869.
Chiapaneco: The Chiapanecs were an Otomanguean people of the Grijalva valley in Chiapas, Mexico.
Chibuleo: The Chibuleo are a Kichwa community of Tungurahua, Ecuador.
Chichas: The Chichas were an Andean people of southern Bolivia who served the Inca as soldiers.
Chickahominy: The Chickahominy are an Algonquian people of Virginia who kept their independence from the Powhatan chiefdom.
Chickasaw: The Chickasaw are a Muskogean people of northern Mississippi, known as formidable warriors.
Chickasaw (Oklahoma): Lands in Oklahoma assigned to the Chickasaw Nation after their forced removal in the 1830s.
Chicora: The Chicora were a Siouan people of the South Carolina coast who met Spanish slave raiders in 1521.
Chikashsha Yaki (Chickasaw): Chikashsha Yaki is the homeland of the Chickasaw Nation in the upper Tombigbee region.
Chile: Chile became independent in 1818 and won the nitrate-rich Atacama in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884).
Chilula: The Chilula were an Athabaskan people of Redwood Creek in northwest California.
Chimacum: The Chimakum were a small people of the Olympic Peninsula whose language was related to Quileute.
Chimariko (territory): The Chimariko were a small people of the Trinity River in California, with a language unrelated to their neighbours'.
Chimú: The Chimú kingdom of Peru's north coast ruled from the adobe city of Chan Chan. The Inca conquered it around 1470.
Chimú Empire: The Kingdom of Chimor ruled about 1,000 km of the Peruvian coast from Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas.
China: The Republic of China (from 1912) and the People's Republic of China (from 1949). Mao proclaimed the People's Republic on 1 October 1949.
Chinantla (Tsa ju jmí’): The Chinantec are an Otomanguean people of northern Oaxaca, Mexico, who speak a whistled form of their language.
Chinchoros: The Chinchorro fishers of the Atacama coast made the world's oldest known artificial mummies, about 2,000 years before Egypt.
Chinchorro culture: The Chinchorro culture of northern Chile and southern Peru mummified its dead from about 5000 BC.
Chinese warlords: After 1916, regional military cliques divided China, and the Nationalist government only partly brought them under its control.
Chinook: The Chinook were traders of the lower Columbia River. Their trade jargon became the common language of the Pacific Northwest.
Chiquitano: The Chiquitano live in the Chiquitos lowlands of Bolivia, home to Jesuit mission churches built in the 1700s.
Chiricahua: The Chiricahua Apache of southeast Arizona and northern Mexico were led in the 1800s by Cochise and Geronimo.
Chiricahua Apache: The Chiricahua Apache were the band of Cochise and Geronimo, the last Native Americans to surrender to the US Army, in 1886.
Chiso: The Chisos were a Concho-speaking people of the Big Bend region of Texas and Chihuahua.
Chisos: The Chisos were a people of the Big Bend country on the Rio Grande; the Chisos Mountains are named after them.
Chit-dee-ni (Chetco): The Chetco are an Athabaskan people of the southern Oregon coast.
Chitimacha: The Chitimacha are a people of the Mississippi delta in Louisiana, known for their double-woven cane baskets.
Chitonahua/Murunahua: The Chitonahua are a small Panoan people of the upper Yurúa river in Peru.
Chochenyo: The Chochenyo are an Ohlone people of the East Bay, around today's Oakland, California.
Choctaw: The Choctaw were a large Muskogean nation of Mississippi and Alabama, removed to Oklahoma in 1831–1833.
Choctaw (Oklahoma): The reservation lands of the Choctaw Nation in southeast Oklahoma.
Chola Empire: The Cholas of Thanjavur were a Tamil dynasty. Around 1025 Rajendra I sent a navy to raid Srivijaya across the Bay of Bengal.
Cholulteca: The people of Cholula, a Nahua city near Puebla with the largest pyramid by volume in the world.
Chono: The Chono were canoe nomads of the Chilean fjords and the Chonos Archipelago.
Chontal de Guerrero – Tuxteco: A Chontal community of the Guerrero highlands in Mexico.
Chopcca: The Chopcca are a Quechua community of Huancavelica, Peru, known for traditional dress.
Chorotega: The Chorotega were Otomanguean farmers of Nicaragua's Pacific coast and the Nicoya Peninsula.
Chorrera: The Chorrera culture of coastal Ecuador made fine pottery, including whistling bottles, between about 1300 and 300 BC.
Chowanoke: The Chowanoke were an Algonquian people of the Chowan River in North Carolina.
Chtimacha: The Chitimacha are a Louisiana delta people, among the region's oldest and the only ones to keep part of their ancestral land.
Chuds: The Chuds were Finnic peoples of the north Russian forests, named in early Rus' chronicles.
Chukchansi: The Chukchansi are a Yokuts people of the Sierra Nevada foothills, California.
Chukchi: The Chukchi are reindeer herders and sea hunters of Siberia's far northeast. Russian forces spent much of the 1700s trying to conquer them and failed.
Chumash: The Chumash of the Santa Barbara coast built plank canoes and traded shell-bead money.
Chūzan: Chūzan was one of three kingdoms on Okinawa. It united the island as the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1429.
Ciboney: The Ciboney were early fishing and gathering peoples of western Cuba and Hispaniola.
Ciguayo: The Ciguayo were a people of northeastern Hispaniola. They fought Columbus's men in 1493, the first battle between Europeans and Americans.
Cimmerians: The Cimmerians were steppe horsemen north of the Black Sea who invaded Anatolia in the 700s BC.
Circars: The Northern Circars were districts on India's east coast, given to the East India Company in 1766.
Clackamas: The Clackamas were a Chinookan people of the Clackamas River near Portland, Oregon.
Clatskanie: The Clatskanie were an Athabaskan people of the hills above the lower Columbia River.
Clatsop: The Clatsop were a Chinookan people near the mouth of the Columbia, where Lewis and Clark spent the winter of 1805–1806.
Coahuiltec: The Coahuiltecan peoples were hunter-gatherers of south Texas and northeast Mexico, made up of many small bands.
Coahuiltecan: The Coahuiltecan peoples were mobile foragers of the Rio Grande plains.
Coast Salish: The Coast Salish peoples of the Salish Sea live on salmon and cedar and build large plank houses.
Coast Yuki: The Coast Yuki were a small people of the Mendocino coast in California.
Coastal and Woodland Mesolithic Hunter-F: These were the Natufian and post-Natufian foragers of the Levant, among the first people to live year-round in villages.
Coca: The Coca were a Nahuatl-related people of the Lake Chapala region, Jalisco.
Cochimí: The Cochimí were hunter-gatherers of the central Baja California desert, known for great rock-art murals.
Cochin: The Kingdom of Cochin was a pepper port on the Kerala coast, allied first with Portugal and then with the Dutch.
Cochin China: Cochinchina was the European name for southern Vietnam. France conquered it in 1859–1867 and made it a colony.
Coharie: The Coharie are a Native community of the Coharie River in North Carolina.
Colchis: Colchis was a kingdom on the east coast of the Black Sea, in western Georgia. It was the land of the Golden Fleece in Greek myth.
Colombia: Colombia was the core of Bolívar's Gran Colombia. Panama broke away with US support in 1903.
Colville: The Colville Confederated Tribes are Interior Salish peoples of northeast Washington.
Comanche: The Comanche built a horse-powered empire, the Comanchería, across the southern Plains in the 1700s.
Comca’ac (Seri): The Comcaac (Seri) are hunter-fishers of the Sonoran coast of the Gulf of California.
Comté de Toulouse: The County of Toulouse was a powerful southern French lordship that the Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) broke.
Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde: The Grand Ronde Confederated Tribes unite over 30 western Oregon peoples moved to a reservation in the 1850s.
Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians: The Siletz confederation unites many coastal Oregon and northern California peoples moved to the Siletz reservation.
Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs: The Warm Springs, Wasco and Paiute peoples of central Oregon share this reservation.
Confederated Villages of Lisjan: The Lisjan (Ohlone) villages of the East Bay, around today's Oakland and San Leandro, California.
Congaree: The Congaree were a Siouan people of central South Carolina.
Congo: The Kingdom of Kongo, at the mouth of the Congo River, converted to Christianity after Portuguese contact in 1483.
The Kongo kingdom survived as a Portuguese vassal. North of the river, Brazzaville's French Congo later took the name Republic of the Congo (1960).
Congo Free State: King Leopold II of Belgium ran the Congo as his personal possession. Its forced rubber labour killed millions, and Belgium took it over in 1908.
Conoy: The Conoy (Piscataway) were Algonquian people of the Potomac in Maryland.
Coos, Lower Umpqua, Siuslaw: Three small peoples of the central Oregon coast, now a confederated tribe.
Copena: Copena was a Middle Woodland burial-mound culture of the Tennessee valley in Alabama.
Copuces: A small Indigenous people of Jalisco in western Mexico.
Coqs: The source map uses this label for peoples of the lower Columbia River and the Oregon and Washington coast.
Coquille: The Coquille are a people of the Coquille River on the southern Oregon coast.
Coree: The Coree were a small Algonquian-speaking people of the North Carolina coast.
Corsica: Corsica was ruled by Pisa and then by Genoa from 1284, and sold to France in 1768, a year before Napoleon was born there.
Costa Rica: Costa Rica became independent in 1821 and abolished its army in 1948.
Costanoan: The Costanoan (Ohlone) peoples of the San Francisco and Monterey bays lived in many small villages.
Cotonou: Cotonou was a lagoon port of Dahomey ceded to France in 1878, now the largest city of Benin.
Couture Complex: Couture is a Middle Woodland culture of southwestern Ontario and southeastern Michigan.
Cow Creek Umpqua: The Cow Creek band of Umpqua are a people of southwestern Oregon.
Cowlitz: The Cowlitz are a Salish people of the Cowlitz River in southwest Washington.
Coyutecos (Nahua): A Nahua community of the Pacific highlands of western Mexico.
Cree: The Cree are an Algonquian people of the boreal forest from Quebec to Alberta and key partners in the Hudson's Bay Company fur trade.
Crete: Crete held independent Greek city-states in the Hellenistic period, famous for their mercenaries and pirates.
Crimean Khanate: The Crimean Khanate was a Tatar successor of the Golden Horde and an Ottoman vassal from 1475. Russia annexed it in 1783.
Croatan: The Croatan were a Carolina Algonquian people of the Outer Banks. "CROATOAN" was carved at the abandoned Roanoke colony.
Croatia: Croatia was a medieval kingdom that joined Hungary in 1102. It became independent from Yugoslavia in 1991.
Croatian kingdom: Tomislav was crowned the first king of Croatia around 925.
Crow: The Crow (Apsáalooke) were horse-rich Plains people of the Yellowstone country.
Cuba: Cuba became independent in 1902 after the US defeated Spain. Fidel Castro's revolution took power in 1959.
Cuba (Spain): Cuba was Spain's richest Caribbean colony. Havana was where the treasure fleets gathered before crossing the Atlantic.
Cuica: The Cuica were Timote-speaking farmers of the Venezuelan Andes.
Cuitlatec: The Cuitlatec were a people of Guerrero, Mexico, with a language unrelated to any other.
Cuman Khanates: The Cumans (Kipchaks) were Turkic nomads of the steppe from the Danube to the Volga before the Mongols.
Cuman-Kipchak confederation: The Cuman-Kipchak confederation was a loose Turkic league that dominated the western steppe from the 1000s.
Cupeño: The Cupeño are a small people of the hot springs of Warner's Ranch in southern California.
Curonians: The Curonians were a Baltic people of the Latvian and Lithuanian coast, known as sea raiders. Courland is named after them.
Cusabo: The Cusabo were peoples of the South Carolina Lowcountry; the source map places this label in southern New England, where the Narragansett and Wampanoag lived.
Cushites: Cushitic-speaking herders of the Horn of Africa, ancestors of the Somali and Oromo.
Cuttatawomen: The Cuttatawomen were a Powhatan-allied people of the Rappahannock River in Virginia.
Cuxhaven: Cuxhaven was a small exclave of Hamburg at the mouth of the Elbe.
Cycladic: The Cycladic culture of the Aegean islands made the famous flat marble figurines of the Early Bronze Age.
Cyprus: Cyprus was ruled in turn by Byzantium, Crusader kings, Venice, the Ottomans and Britain. It became independent in 1960.
Cyrenaica: Cyrenaica is eastern Libya, an Ottoman province governed through the Karamanli pashas of Tripoli in the 1700s.
Cyrenaica (British administration): Britain ran Cyrenaica after defeating Italy in 1942–1943, before Libya's independence in 1951.
Czech Republic: The Czech Republic was formed when Czechoslovakia split peacefully on 1 January 1993.
Czechoslovakia: Czechoslovakia was created in 1918 from Austria-Hungary's lands. It lost the Sudetenland to Germany in 1938.
Czechs: Czechs were West Slavic tribes who settled Bohemia in the 500s and 600s and later formed the Přemyslid state.
Dacia: Dacia was the gold-rich kingdom of Decebalus in today's Romania. Trajan conquered it in 106.
Dacians: The Dacians were Thracian-related peoples north of the Danube, united under King Burebista around 60 BC.
Dadi Dadi: The Dadi Dadi are Aboriginal people of the Murray River near Euston, New South Wales.
Dahomey: Dahomey was a West African kingdom at Abomey, famous for its women soldiers. France conquered it in 1892–1894.
Dahomey was a French colony that became independent in 1960 and was renamed Benin in 1975.
Dainggatti: The Dainggatti are Aboriginal people of the Macleay River on the mid-north coast of New South Wales.
Dakapeng culture: The Dapenkeng culture was the first pottery-making culture of Taiwan, often linked to the origin of Austronesian languages.
Dakeł Keyoh (ᑕᗸᒡ ᗲᘏᑋ): The homeland of the Dakelh (Carrier), a Dene people of central British Columbia.
Dali Kingdom: The Dali Kingdom was a Bai-led Buddhist kingdom in Yunnan from 937, until the Mongols conquered it in 1253.
Damot: Dʿmt was a kingdom of Eritrea and northern Ethiopia in the first millennium BC, with close ties to Saba in Yemen.
Danes: Danes were the Norse people of Jutland and the Danish islands. Their Vikings raided and settled England.
Dangbon: The Dangbon are Aboriginal people of western Arnhem Land.
Danggali: The Danggali are Aboriginal people of the dry country along the South Australia–New South Wales border.
Danish West Indies: The Danish West Indies were sugar islands of St. Thomas, St. John and St. Croix, sold to the United States in 1917.
Danube Bulgars: The Danube Bulgars founded the First Bulgarian Empire south of the Danube in 681.
Danzig: The Free City of Danzig was a League of Nations protectorate from 1920. Germany's attack here began World War II in 1939.
Dapenkeng culture: The Dapenkeng culture was the earliest Neolithic culture of Taiwan, from about 4000 BC.
Dardania: Dardania was an Illyrian–Thracian kingdom in today's Kosovo and North Macedonia.
Darfur: The Keira Sultanate of Darfur ruled from Jebel Marra from the 1600s until Egypt conquered it in 1874.
Darkinung: The Darkinjung are Aboriginal people of the Hawkesbury and Central Coast north of Sydney.
Darumbal: The Darumbal are Aboriginal people of the Rockhampton area, Queensland.
Dau Nom Wintu: A Wintu band of the upper Sacramento valley in northern California.
Dau Pom Wintu: A Wintu band of the McCloud River in northern California.
Da’naxda’xw Awaetlatla: The Da'naxda'xw Awaetlatla are a Kwakwaka'wakw nation of Knight Inlet, British Columbia.
Deccan kingdoms: The Ikshvakus, Vakatakas and early Pallavas split the Deccan after the Satavahanas.
Deg Xit'an Ngan' (Deg Xit'an): The Deg Xit'an are a Dene people of the lower Yukon River in Alaska.
Dehcho Dene: The Dehcho Dene are Dene people of the Mackenzie River (Deh Cho) in the Northwest Territories.
Delagoa Bay: Delagoa Bay is a Portuguese trading post on the Mozambique coast, today's Maputo.
Delaware: The Lenape (Delaware) are Algonquian people of the Delaware River valley who signed William Penn's treaty of 1682.
Democratic Republic of the Congo: Zaire was renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1997, after Mobutu's fall. The war of 1998–2003 drew in nine African countries.
Dena'ina Ełnena: The Dena'ina are Dene people of Cook Inlet and the Anchorage area of Alaska.
Dendi Kingdom: Dendi was the southern remnant of the Songhai Empire on the Niger, which held out after Morocco's conquest of 1591.
Dene Tha': The Dene Tha' are a Dene people of northwest Alberta.
Denendeh (Dënësųłinë́ Nëné): The homeland of the Dënësųłinë́ (Chipewyan), Dene people of the taiga west of Hudson Bay.
Deni: The Deni are an Arawan people of the Purus and Juruá basins in the Brazilian Amazon.
Denmark: Denmark is one of Europe's oldest kingdoms. In the 1000s its kings Sweyn and Cnut also ruled England.
Denmark-Norway: Norway was joined to Denmark from 1380 (formally from 1536) until 1814, along with Iceland, Greenland and the Faroes.
Derbent: Derbent is a fortress city on the Caspian, where the Caucasus meets the sea. It was the gateway between the steppe and Persia.
Desert hunter-gatherers: Hunter-gatherers of the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts, who lived on mesquite, agave and small game.
Dharawala: The Dharawal are Aboriginal people of central Queensland.
Dharug: The Darug are Aboriginal people of the Sydney plains; the first British colony was founded on their land in 1788.
Dhirari: The Dhirari are Aboriginal people near Lake Eyre, South Australia.
Diaguita: The Diaguita were farming peoples of northwest Argentina and northern Chile who resisted the Spanish in the Calchaquí wars.
Dieri: The Dieri are Aboriginal people of the Cooper Creek country east of Lake Eyre.
Dimini: Dimini is a Neolithic hilltop settlement in Thessaly with stone ring walls, one of Europe's earliest.
Diné Bikéyah: Diné Bikéyah is the homeland of the Diné (Navajo), between their four sacred mountains.
Ditidaht: The Ditidaht are a Nuu-chah-nulth people of southwest Vancouver Island.
Dja Dja Wurrung: The Dja Dja Wurrung are Kulin people of the central Victorian goldfields.
Djabuganjdji: The Djabugay are Aboriginal people of the Kuranda rainforest near Cairns.
Djabwurung: The Djab Wurrung are Aboriginal people of the Grampians in western Victoria.
Djargurdwurung: The Djargurd Wurrung are Aboriginal people of the Lake Corangamite area, Victoria.
Djeoromitxí: The Djeoromitxí (Jabutí) are a small Macro-Jê people of Rondônia, Brazil.
Djibouti: French Somaliland became independent as Djibouti in 1977, a strategic port at the mouth of the Red Sea.
Djirbalngan: The Jirrbal are rainforest Aboriginal people of the Atherton Tableland.
Dodecanese Islands: The Dodecanese, including Rhodes, were Italian from 1912 to 1947, then passed to Greece.
Doeg: The Doeg were an Algonquian people of northern Virginia on the Potomac.
Dokapuara (Tuyuca): The Tuyuca are a Tukanoan people of the Vaupés region on the Colombia–Brazil border.
Dominica: Dominica was the last Caribbean island to be colonised because of fierce Kalinago resistance. It became independent in 1978.
Dominican Republic: The Dominican Republic won independence from Haiti in 1844.
Dominion of Newfoundland: Newfoundland was a self-governing dominion that gave up self-rule in 1934 during the Depression and joined Canada in 1949.
Donghu tribes: The Donghu ("Eastern Hu") were nomads of eastern Mongolia, ancestors of the Xianbei and Wuhuan.
Doolboong/Miriwoong: The Miriwoong are Aboriginal people of the Kununurra area in the east Kimberley.
Dorset: The Dorset culture was a Paleo-Inuit Arctic culture, replaced by the ancestors of the Inuit (Thule) after about 1000.
Dravidians: Dravidian-speaking peoples of South Asia, whose languages (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) predate Indo-Aryan in India.
Duchy of Benevento: Benevento was a Lombard principality of southern Italy that outlasted the Lombard kingdom in the north.
Duchy of Swabia: Swabia was one of the stem duchies of medieval Germany, later held by the Hohenstaufen dynasty.
Dumnonia: Dumnonia was a British kingdom of Devon and Cornwall that held out against the Anglo-Saxons into the 800s.
Dumonii: The Dumnonii were the Celtic people of Devon and Cornwall in Roman times.
Durdzuks: The Durdzuks were the medieval name for the Vainakh, ancestors of the Chechens and Ingush.
Dutch Brazil: The Dutch West India Company held northeast Brazil, around Recife, from 1630 to 1654.
Dutch East Indies: The Dutch East India Company and then the Dutch state ruled the Indonesian islands for spices, sugar and coffee.
Dutch Formosa: The Dutch ruled southwest Taiwan from Fort Zeelandia (1624–1662) until Koxinga drove them out.
Dutch Guiana: Dutch Guiana (Suriname) was a plantation colony on the South American coast that the Dutch kept in exchange for New Amsterdam in 1667.
Dutch Republic: The Dutch Republic won independence from Spain after the Eighty Years' War (1568–1648) and became Europe's leading trading power.
Dutch settlements: Dutch-speaking farmers (Boers) on the eastern frontier of the Cape Colony.
Duwamish: The Duwamish are a Coast Salish people of the Seattle area. The city is named after their leader Si'ahl.
Dvaravati: Dvaravati was a Mon Buddhist civilisation of central Thailand from the 500s to the 1000s.
Dyo'xaiya-o-Ivo'tsa (Okaina): The Ocaina are a Witotoan people of the Ampiyacu river in the Peruvian Amazon.
Dyungungoo (Gubbi Gubbi): The Kabi Kabi (Gubbi Gubbi) are Aboriginal people of the Sunshine Coast in Queensland.
Dâw: The Dâw are a small Nadahup people of the Rio Negro near São Gabriel da Cachoeira, Brazil.
Dënéndeh: Denendeh, "land of the people", is the homeland of the Dene peoples of northwest Canada.
E'ñepá: The E'ñepá (Panare) are a Carib-speaking people of the Venezuelan llanos and Guiana highlands.
Early Indus farming cultures: Farming villages of the Indus region and Baluchistan, such as Mehrgarh, that led to the Indus cities.
Early Nile valley cultures: These were early farming cultures of the Nile valley, before the Naqada period.
Early combware: Comb Ceramic hunter-fishers of northeast Europe decorated their pottery with comb impressions.
East Francia: East Francia was the eastern part of Charlemagne's empire. It became the Kingdom of Germany and, from 962, the Holy Roman Empire.
East Germany: The German Democratic Republic was the Soviet-backed state founded in 1949. It built the Berlin Wall in 1961.
East Getaes: The Geats of Östergötland in southern Sweden, the people of the hero Beowulf.
East Java: East Javanese kingdoms such as Kahuripan and Kediri succeeded Mataram after the court moved east around 929.
East Prussia: East Prussia was cut off from the rest of Germany by the Polish Corridor after 1919, and divided between Poland and the USSR in 1945.
Eastern Masurian culture: An Iron Age West Baltic culture of the Masurian lakes in northeastern Poland.
Eastern Mono/Monache: The Monache are a Western Mono people of the Sierra Nevada foothills in California.
Eastern Nehântick: The Eastern Niantic were an Algonquian people of the Rhode Island coast.
Eastern New Guinea: New Guinea held hundreds of Papuan and Austronesian societies, and some of the world's earliest farming, around 7000 BC in the highlands.
Eastern North American hunter-gatherers: Archaic and Woodland foragers of the eastern forests, who domesticated squash and sunflower.
Eastern Pomo: The Eastern Pomo are a Pomoan people of Clear Lake in California.
Eastern Roman Empire: The Eastern Roman Empire ruled from Constantinople after 395. Justinian (527–565) won back Italy and North Africa.
Eastern Shawnee (Oklahoma): The Oklahoma lands of the Eastern Shawnee Tribe, who were removed west from Ohio in the 1830s.
Eastern Shoshone: The Eastern Shoshone are Plains Shoshone of the Wind River country in Wyoming, led in the 1800s by Chief Washakie.
Ecuador: Ecuador left Gran Colombia in 1830. It is named after the equator, which runs through it.
Ecuana: A small Indigenous territory of the Bolivian lowlands.
Eduria (Taiwano): The Eduria (Taiwano) are a Tukanoan people of the Colombian Vaupés.
Eeyou Istchee: Eeyou Istchee is the homeland of the Eastern James Bay Cree in Quebec.
Egypt: Egypt was unified around 3100 BC and ruled by pharaohs for three thousand years.
Arab armies conquered Egypt in 639–642. The Ottomans ruled it from 1517, then Muhammad Ali's dynasty from 1805, under British occupation from 1882.
Egyptian Somali coast: Khedive Ismail's Egypt held Zeila, Berbera and Harar between 1870 and 1884, before withdrawing during the Mahdist war.
El Paraiso: El Paraíso is a monumental stone complex near Lima from about 2000 BC, one of the Americas' earliest.
El Pom Wintu: A Wintu band of the upper Sacramento River in northern California.
El Salvador: El Salvador is the smallest Central American country, independent since 1821 and a separate republic from 1841.
Elam: Elam was an ancient kingdom of southwest Iran with its capital at Susa, a rival of Mesopotamia for 2,000 years.
Electoral Hesse: Hesse-Kassel was a German state whose rulers held the title of Elector from 1803. Prussia annexed it in 1866.
Emberá: The Emberá are a Chocó people of the Panama–Colombia rainforest who live in houses on stilts.
Emberá Chamí: The Emberá Chamí are an Emberá people of the Colombian Andes.
Emberá Dobidá: The Emberá Dobidá ("river people") live along the Atrato and Baudó rivers in Colombia.
Emberá Katío/Eyabida: The Emberá Katío live in the Sinú and Atrato river headwaters of Colombia.
Emberá/Eperara/Épera: The Emberá peoples of Colombia's Pacific lowlands share a family of Chocó languages.
Emirate of Córdoba: Abd al-Rahman I, an Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasids, founded an independent emirate in al-Andalus in 756.
Emirate of Jabal Shammar: The Rashidi dynasty of Ha'il ruled northern Arabia, rivals of the Saudis until Ibn Saud took Ha'il in 1921.
Emirate of Sicily: The Aghlabids conquered Sicily from 827. Under Arab rule Palermo became a great city of irrigated gardens.
Emirate of Tiflis: The Emirate of Tiflis was an Arab emirate in Tbilisi from 736, until Georgia's King David IV took the city back in 1122.
Emirate of the White Sheep Turks: The Aq Qoyunlu were a Turkmen confederation that ruled Iran and Anatolia. Uzun Hasan defeated their Black Sheep rivals in 1467.
Empire of Alexander: Alexander of Macedon conquered the Persian Empire in eleven years. He died in Babylon in June 323 BC, aged 32.
Empire of Brazil: Emperor Pedro II ruled Brazil for 58 years and abolished slavery in 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so. A republican coup deposed him the next year.
Empire of Ghana: The Ghana Empire (Wagadu) grew rich on trans-Saharan gold; Arab writers called it "the land of gold".
Empire of Japan: The Empire of Japan was the Meiji-era state that won Taiwan (1895) and Korea (1910) and fought World War II.
Enawenê-nawê: The Enawenê-nawê are an Arawakan people of Mato Grosso, Brazil, who live mainly by fishing and do not eat red meat.
Enenlhet-Toba: The Toba-Maskoy are an Enlhet–Enenlhet people of the Paraguayan Chaco.
Enets: The Enets are a small Samoyedic people of the Yenisei estuary in Siberia.
