England: England was unified in the 900s. The Normans conquered it in 1066.
England and Ireland: The Tudor and Stuart kings ruled England and claimed Ireland. Henry VIII took the title King of Ireland in 1542.
English territory: Lands held by the English crown in Plantagenet times, including Wales after Edward I's conquest in 1283.
Enlhet: The Enlhet are a people of the central Paraguayan Chaco.
Enlhet-Enenlhet: The Enlhet–Enenlhet language family includes several Chaco peoples of Paraguay.
Eno: The Eno were a Siouan people of the North Carolina Piedmont.
Entiat: The Entiat are a Salish band of the Entiat River in Washington.
Envuga (Kawahib): A Tupi–Kawahib group of Rondônia in Brazil.
Enxet: The Enxet are a people of the lower Paraguayan Chaco.
Eora: The Eora are the Aboriginal people of the Sydney Harbour coast, the first to meet the British colonists in 1788.
Eperara Siapidara: The Eperara Siapidara are an Emberá people of the Colombian Pacific coast.
Equatorial Guinea: Spanish Guinea became independent as Equatorial Guinea in 1968, the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa.
Erie: The Erie were Iroquoian farmers south of Lake Erie, destroyed by the Haudenosaunee in the 1650s.
Eritrea: Eritrea was an Italian colony from 1890. It was federated with Ethiopia, annexed, and won independence in 1993 after a 30-year war.
Esketemculeucw (Esk'etemc): The Esk'etemc are a Secwépemc (Shuswap) community of the Fraser River near Alkali Lake, British Columbia.
Esse ejja: The Ese Ejja are a Tacanan people of the rivers of the Bolivia–Peru Amazon.
Esselen: The Esselen were a small people of the Big Sur coast in California.
Essequibo: Essequibo was a Dutch plantation colony on the Essequibo River, later part of British Guiana.
Essex: Essex was the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the East Saxons, which included London for a time.
Estonia: Estonia won independence from Russia in 1918–1920, was annexed by the USSR in 1940, and became independent again in 1991.
Ests: The Ests were the Finnic people of Estonia. Danish and German crusaders conquered them in the 1200s.
Ethiopia: The Solomonic dynasty restored by Yekuno Amlak in 1270 ruled Ethiopia, which was never colonised apart from Italy's occupation of 1936–1941.
Ethiopian Highland Peoples: Peoples of the Ethiopian plateau around the Aksumite kingdom's southern frontier.
Ethiopian highland farmers: Highland farmers of Ethiopia who domesticated teff, coffee and enset.
Etrurians: The Etruscans were a pre-Roman people of Tuscany who taught Rome much of its religion and engineering.
Eyak: The Eyak were a people of the Copper River delta. Their last native speaker died in 2008.
Eyaq: The Eyak lived on the Gulf of Alaska coast near Cordova, between the Tlingit and the Alutiiq.
Fante: The Fante are an Akan people of the Gold Coast. Their coastal states allied with Britain against Asante.
Far Eastern Republic: The Far Eastern Republic was a Soviet buffer state in eastern Siberia (1920–1922), meant to avoid war with Japan.
Fatimid Caliphate: The Fatimids were Ismaili Shia caliphs who founded Cairo in 969 and Al-Azhar soon after.
Fernandeño Tataviam: The Tataviam lived in the Santa Clarita and San Fernando valleys of southern California.
Fezzan (French administration): France administered the Fezzan in southwest Libya from 1943 until Libyan independence in 1951.
Fiji: Fiji became a British colony in 1874. Britain brought Indian indentured labourers to work the sugar fields, and the country became independent in 1970.
Finland: Finland was a Swedish land for 600 years and a Russian grand duchy from 1809. It became independent in December 1917.
Finnmark: Finnmark is Norway's Arctic north, a Sámi land disputed with Russia and Sweden until borders were fixed in 1751 and 1826.
Finno-Ugric taiga hunter-gatherers: Forest hunters and fishers of the northern Urals and Siberia, ancestors of Uralic-speaking peoples.
Finns: Finnic peoples of southern Finland, who traded furs with the Vikings and Novgorod.
First Bulgarian Empire: The First Bulgarian Empire adopted Christianity in 864 and the Cyrillic alphabet soon after. Byzantium conquered it in 1018.
Fivizzano: Fivizzano is a small Lunigiana town that belonged to Florence and then the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.
Flathead: The Bitterroot Salish (Flathead) of western Montana met Lewis and Clark in 1805.
Florence: Florence was the city-state of the Medici and the cradle of the Renaissance. It became the Grand Duchy of Tuscany in 1569.
Florida: Spanish Florida was centred on St. Augustine, founded in 1565, the oldest European city in the US.
Florida (Spain): Spain traded Florida to Britain in 1763, recovered it in 1783, and sold it to the US in 1821.
Fort Ancient culture: The Fort Ancient culture was made up of maize farmers of the Ohio valley who lived from about 1000 to 1750, probably ancestors of the Shawnee.
Fourche Maline Culture: Fourche Maline was a Woodland culture of eastern Oklahoma and Arkansas, ancestral to the Caddo.
Fox: The Meskwaki (Fox) were an Algonquian people of Wisconsin who fought the French in the Fox Wars (1712–1733).
France: The Capetian kings built France outward from Paris. Under Louis XIV (1643–1715) it was Europe's leading power.
Franche-Comté: The Franche-Comté was a Habsburg county in eastern France that Louis XIV conquered in 1674.
Frankish Kingdom: The Merovingian kings ruled Gaul after Clovis, who was baptised around 500.
Franks: The Franks were a Germanic confederation of the lower Rhine. Clovis united them around 500.
French Cameroons: French Cameroons was a League of Nations mandate taken from Germany after World War I. It became independent in 1960.
French Cochinchina and Cambodia: France annexed southern Vietnam (1862–1867) and made Cambodia a protectorate (1863).
French Congo: French Congo was the colony founded by Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza in the 1880s, with its capital at Brazzaville.
French Equatorial Africa: French Equatorial Africa was a federation of Gabon, Middle Congo, Ubangi-Shari and Chad, from 1910 to 1958.
French Guiana: French Guiana is France's South American department, home to the Kourou spaceport since 1968.
French Indochina: French Indochina was a union of Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos formed in 1887. It broke up after the Indochina War of 1946–1954.
French Somaliland: French Somaliland was the port of Djibouti at the mouth of the Red Sea, end point of the railway from Addis Ababa.
French Sudan: French Sudan was the colony on the upper Niger that became Mali in 1960.
French Togoland: French Togoland was the eastern part of German Togo, mandated to France after 1919. It became independent as Togo in 1960.
French West Africa: French West Africa was a federation of eight colonies governed from Dakar, from 1895 to 1958.
Frisians: The Frisians were North Sea coastal traders of the Low Countries, who built mounds (terpen) against floods.
Funan: Funan was the earliest known state of mainland Southeast Asia, in the Mekong delta. Its port at Óc Eo traded with India and Rome.
Funj: The Funj Sultanate of Sennar ruled the Nile between the cataracts and Ethiopia from about 1504 to 1821.
Funnel-Beaker: The Funnel Beaker culture was the first farming culture of northern Europe and built many megalithic tombs.
Futa Jalon: Futa Jallon was an Islamic Fula state in the Guinea highlands, founded in the 1720s.
Futa Toro: Futa Toro was a Fula Islamic state on the middle Senegal River, the homeland of El Hadj Umar Tall.
Féénemɨnaa: A small Witotoan people of the Colombian Amazon.
Gabalbara: The Gabalbara are Aboriginal people of central Queensland.
Gabon: Gabon was a French colony on the equator, part of French Equatorial Africa, and became independent in 1960.
Gadubanud: The Gadubanud are Aboriginal people of the Otway coast in Victoria.
Gaelic Ireland: Early medieval Ireland had many Gaelic kingdoms and great monasteries that preserved Latin learning.
Gagudju: The Gagudju are Aboriginal people of Kakadu (named after them) in the Northern Territory.
Gahadavala dynasty: The Gahadavalas ruled Kannauj and Varanasi until Muhammad of Ghor defeated them in 1194.
Gamberre: The Gambera are Aboriginal people of the north Kimberley coast.
Gambia: Gambia is Britain's narrow colony along the Gambia River, the oldest British possession in Africa.
Gambia, The: The Gambia is a British colony along the Gambia River, completely surrounded by Senegal. It became independent in 1965.
Gananggalinda: A small Aboriginal group of the Gulf of Carpentaria coast.
Gandhara grave culture: The Gandhara grave culture was a Late Bronze Age culture of the Swat valley in Pakistan, sometimes linked to early Indo-Aryans.
Gandhāra: Gandhara was a Persian satrapy around Taxila and Peshawar, later famous for Greco-Buddhist sculpture.
Ganggalida: The Ganggalida (Yukulta) are Aboriginal people of the southern Gulf of Carpentaria.
Gangulu: The Gangulu are Aboriginal people of the Dawson River, Queensland.
Garawa: The Garrwa are Aboriginal people of the Gulf country on the Northern Territory–Queensland border.
Garingbal: The Karingbal are Aboriginal people of the Carnarvon Gorge region, Queensland.
Garrochambas: A small Andean community territory in southern Ecuador.
Garífuna: The Garifuna formed on Saint Vincent in the 1600s from Africans and Island Caribs. Britain exiled them to the Honduran coast in 1797, so this 1492 label is anachronistic.
Gauda Kingdom: King Shashanka of Gauda (Bengal) was a rival of Emperor Harsha in the early 600s.
Gaya: Gaya was a confederacy of iron-producing city-states in southern Korea. Silla absorbed it in 562.
Gayiri: The Kairi are Aboriginal people of central Queensland.
Geats: The Geats of southern Sweden were the people of the Beowulf poem.
Geawegal: The Geawegal are Aboriginal people of the upper Hunter River, New South Wales.
Geneva: Geneva was the Protestant city-republic of Calvin, allied with the Swiss.
Genoa: Genoa was a maritime republic and Venice's rival, with colonies in Corsica, Crimea and the Aegean. Its bankers financed Spain.
Georgia: Georgia was a Christian Caucasus kingdom at its height under Queen Tamar (1184–1213). It was annexed by Russia in 1801.
Georgian Kingdom: The Georgian kingdoms of Kartli and Iberia lived under Byzantine and Arab overlords.
Gepids: The Gepids were an East Germanic people of the Carpathian Basin, subjects of the Huns, then rivals of the Lombards.
German E. Africa (Tanganyika): German East Africa was Germany's largest colony. Its forces under Lettow-Vorbeck fought on unbeaten to the end of World War I.
German East Africa: Germany took the mainland opposite Zanzibar in the 1880s and crushed the Abushiri and Maji Maji revolts.
German Empire: Bismarck united Germany under the Prussian king, proclaimed emperor at Versailles in 1871. It ended in revolution in November 1918.
German South-West Africa: German South-West Africa was a German colony from 1884, where the army killed most of the Herero and Nama in 1904–1908, now recognised as genocide.
German and British New Guinea: From 1884 Germany ruled northeast New Guinea and Britain (later Australia) ruled Papua in the southeast.
Germanic tribes: Iron Age Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia and northern Germany.
Germany: The German Empire (1871–1918), the Weimar and Nazi states, and from 1990 reunified Germany.
Germany (France): The French occupation zone in southwest Germany after 1945.
Germany (Soviet): The Soviet occupation zone in eastern Germany, which became East Germany in 1949.
Germany (UK): The British occupation zone in northwest Germany, including the Ruhr.
Germany (USA): The American occupation zone in southern Germany, including Bavaria.
Ghana: The Gold Coast became Ghana in 1957, the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence, led by Kwame Nkrumah.
Ghana Empire: The Ghana Empire (Wagadu) of the Soninke traded gold for Saharan salt. It declined in the 1100s.
Gharra: A tribal territory of inland Oman named in the source map.
Ghassul: Teleilat Ghassul is a Chalcolithic village near the Dead Sea, known for its painted wall murals.
Ghaznavid Emirate: The Ghaznavids were Turkic sultans of Ghazni. Mahmud (998–1030) raided northern India seventeen times.
Ghurid Sultanate: The Ghurids rose from the mountains of central Afghanistan to conquer northern India in the 1190s.
Gilbert and Ellice Islands: The Gilbert and Ellice Islands were a British Pacific colony. They split in the 1970s into Kiribati and Tuvalu.
Giraiwurung: The Girai Wurrung are Aboriginal people of the Warrnambool coast, Victoria.
Gitanyow Lax’yip: The territory of the Gitanyow, a Gitxsan people of the Kitwanga area in British Columbia.
Gitga’at: The Gitga'at are a Tsimshian people of Hartley Bay on the British Columbia coast.
Gitga’at Lax Yuup: The traditional lands of the Gitga'at Tsimshian of Hartley Bay.
Gitxaała: The Gitxaała are a Tsimshian nation of the outer islands south of Prince Rupert.
Gitx̱san Lax̱yip: The lands of the Gitxsan of the upper Skeena River, famous for their totem poles.
Giya: The Giya are Aboriginal people of the Bowen area in Queensland.
Glades Culture: The Glades culture was made up of fisher-hunters of south Florida's Everglades and coast, ancestors of the Tequesta and Calusa.
Goa: Goa was Portugal's capital in Asia from 1510 until India annexed it in 1961.
Goghtn: Goghtn was an Armenian district on the Aras River, known for its wine and minstrels.
Goguryeo: Goguryeo was one of Korea's Three Kingdoms, ruling Manchuria and northern Korea. Tang China and Silla destroyed it in 668.
Gojoseon: Gojoseon was the first Korean state in tradition. The Han dynasty conquered it in 108 BC.
Golconda: The Qutb Shahi sultanate of Golconda was famous for its diamond mines, which produced the Koh-i-Noor. The Mughals took it in 1687.
Gold Coast: The Gold Coast was a British colony with forts, cocoa farms and gold mines. It became independent as Ghana in 1957.
Golden Horde: The Golden Horde was the western Mongol khanate on the Volga. It ruled the Rus' princes for two centuries, until 1480.
Gondwana: The Gond kingdoms of central India ruled the forested highlands until the Mughals and Marathas took over.
Goodall Focus: Goodall is a Middle Woodland Hopewell-related culture of northern Indiana and southern Michigan.
Gooniyandi: The Gooniyandi are Aboriginal people of the Fitzroy River country in the Kimberley.
Gooty: Gooty is a hill fort in the Deccan held by a Maratha chieftain until Mysore took it in 1775.
Goreng: The Goreng are Noongar people of the south coast of Western Australia.
Goryeo: Goryeo was the Korean dynasty from 918 to 1392 that gave Korea its English name. It printed the Tripitaka Koreana from carved woodblocks.
Goshute: The Goshute are a Western Shoshone people of the Great Basin deserts of Utah.
Goths: The Crimean Goths were a Germanic group who survived in the Crimean mountains into the 1500s.
Granada: The Emirate of Granada was the last Muslim state in Spain, which built the Alhambra. It surrendered in January 1492.
Grand Duchy of Finland: Finland was an autonomous grand duchy of the Russian Empire from 1809 to 1917, with its own parliament.
Grand Duchy of Hesse: Hesse-Darmstadt was a German grand duchy from 1806.
Grand Duchy of Moscow: Moscow rose under the Golden Horde as tax collector for the khans. Ivan III ended tribute to the Horde in 1480.
Graton Rancheria: Federated Coast Miwok and Southern Pomo lands north of San Francisco Bay.
Great Moravia: Great Moravia was the first major West Slavic state. In 863 Saints Cyril and Methodius brought Slavonic-language worship there.
Great Zimbabwe: Great Zimbabwe was a stone-walled capital of a Shona state that traded gold to the Swahili coast. Zimbabwe is named after it.
Greece: Greece won independence from the Ottomans in 1830 and grew in stages until 1947.
Greek city-states: Greek poleis such as Athens, Sparta and Corinth shared a language and gods but rarely a government.
Greek colonies: Greek colonies in southern Italy and Sicily, such as Syracuse and Taras, were so many that the region was called Magna Graecia.
Greenland: Norse settlers lived in Greenland from about 985 to 1450. Denmark–Norway colonised it again from 1721.
Grenada: Grenada is a Caribbean spice island, French until 1763, then British until its independence in 1974.
Griqualand West: Griqualand West was the diamond fields around Kimberley, annexed by Britain in 1871 and joined to the Cape in 1880.
Gros Ventre: The Gros Ventre (Aaniiih) are Algonquian buffalo hunters of the Milk River country in Montana.
Guacata: The Guacata were a people of Florida's Atlantic coast near Cape Canaveral.
Guachichil: The Guachichil were nomadic warriors of the Mexican plateau who fought Spain in the Chichimeca War (1550–1590).
Guachichiles: The Guachichil were the most feared fighters of the Chichimeca War over the Zacatecas silver roads.
Guachimis: A people of the Sonoran Desert in northwest Mexico.
Guadeloupe: Guadeloupe is a French Caribbean sugar colony since 1635, and an overseas department since 1946.
Guahibo/Hiwi: The Sikuani (Guahibo) are mobile people of the Colombian and Venezuelan llanos.
Guajajara: The Guajajara (Tenetehara) are a large Tupi–Guarani people of Maranhão, Brazil.
Guam: Guam was a Spanish colony from 1668 and US territory from 1898. Japan occupied it from 1941 to 1944.
Guamar / Pecchichitane: The Guamares were Chichimeca warriors of the Bajío in central Mexico.
Guamares: The Guamares were Chichimeca hunter-gatherers of Guanajuato.
Guanaca: A small Indigenous community of the Cauca highlands in Colombia.
Guanahatabey: The Guanahatabey were the earliest inhabitants of western Cuba, hunter-gatherers distinct from the Taíno.
Guanahatabeyes: The Guanahatabey were pre-Taíno foragers of Cuba's western tip.
Guanches: The Guanches were the Berber-speaking natives of the Canary Islands. Castile finished conquering them in 1496.
Guane: The Guane were Chibchan farmers of Santander in Colombia, known for cotton textiles.
Guaná: The Guaná are an Arawakan people of the Paraguayan Chaco.
Guarasugwe: The Guarasugwe are a small Tupi–Guarani people of northeastern Bolivia.
Guarayo: The Guarayo are a Tupi–Guarani people of the Bolivian lowlands, gathered into Franciscan missions after 1820.
Guarijío/Guarijó: The Guarijío are a Uto-Aztecan people of the Sierra Madre on the Sonora–Chihuahua border.
Guasaves/Tamazulas: The Guasave were coastal farmers of northern Sinaloa.
Guatemala: Guatemala was the heart of the Spanish Captaincy General of Central America. It became independent in 1821 and a separate republic in 1839.
Guató: The Guató are canoe people of the Pantanal wetlands, Brazil.
Guaycura: The Guaycura were hunter-gatherers of southern Baja California.
Guenoa-Muinanes: The Guenoa were Charrúan hunters of Uruguay and southern Brazil.
Gugu-Badhun: The Gugu-Badhun are Aboriginal people of the upper Burdekin River in north Queensland.
Guinea: Guinea was the only French colony to vote "no" to de Gaulle's community in 1958, and became independent at once.
Guinea-Bissau: Portuguese Guinea won independence as Guinea-Bissau in 1973–1974 after an armed struggle led by Amílcar Cabral.
Guinea-Bissau (Portugal): Portuguese Guinea was a colony of the Cacheu and Bissau trading posts, held by Portugal from the 1400s.
Gujarat: The Gujarat Sultanate grew rich on Indian Ocean trade through ports like Cambay, until Akbar annexed it in 1573.
Gulidjan: The Gulidjan are Aboriginal people of the Lake Colac area, Victoria.
Gumbainggir: The Gumbaynggirr are Aboriginal people of the Coffs Harbour coast, New South Wales.
Guna Yala: Guna Yala is the autonomous Guna region of Panama's San Blas islands, won in the 1925 Guna Revolution.
Guna of Madugandí: Madugandí is a Guna comarca (Indigenous region) in the forests of eastern Panama.
Guna of Wargandí: Wargandí is a Guna comarca in the Darién region of Panama.
Gunadule (Kuna-Tule): The Guna (Kuna) are a Chibchan people of Panama and Colombia, famous for their mola textiles.
Gunbalang: The Kunbarlang are Aboriginal people of western Arnhem Land.
Gunditjmara: The Gunditjmara are Aboriginal people of southwest Victoria. They built stone eel traps at Budj Bim over 6,000 years ago.
Gundungurra: The Gundungurra are Aboriginal people of the Blue Mountains and southern highlands of New South Wales.
Gungabula: The Gungabula are Aboriginal people of the Carnarvon region, Queensland.
Gunggari: The Gunggari are Aboriginal people of the Maranoa River in southern Queensland.
Gungurugoni: The Gurrgoni are Aboriginal people of central Arnhem Land.
Gunibidji: The Gunibidji are Aboriginal people of the Liverpool River in Arnhem Land.
Gunindiri: The Gunindiri are Aboriginal people of the Gulf country, Northern Territory.
Gunu: The Gunu are Aboriginal people of the Warrego River country, Queensland.
Gunwinggu: The Kunwinjku are Aboriginal people of western Arnhem Land, known for x-ray bark painting.
Gupta Empire: The Gupta Empire is often called India's "golden age". Indian mathematicians of the era worked with zero and decimal place value.
Gureng Gureng: The Gurang Gurang are Aboriginal people of the Burnett River area in Queensland.
Gurindji: The Gurindji are Aboriginal people of the Victoria River. Their 1966 Wave Hill walk-off began the Aboriginal land rights movement.
Guringai: The Guringai are Aboriginal people of the northern shores of Sydney Harbour.
Gurjara Pratihara: The Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj held back Arab armies from India in the 700s and 800s.
Guta: The Gutes were the people of Gotland, a Baltic trading island.
Guugu-Yimidhirr: The Guugu Yimithirr live around Cooktown. James Cook recorded their word "kangaroo" there in 1770.
Guwa: The Guwa are Aboriginal people of central-west Queensland.
Guwinmal: The Guwinmal are Aboriginal people of the Shoalwater Bay coast in Queensland.
Guyana: Guyana became independent from Britain in 1966. Venezuela still claims most of it.
Guyana (Netherlands): These were the Dutch plantation colonies of Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice on the Guiana coast.
Gwa’Sala-‘Nakwaxda’xw: The Gwa'sala and 'Nakwaxda'xw are Kwakwaka'wakw peoples of the central British Columbia coast.
Gwich'in Nành: The Gwich'in are Dene caribou hunters of interior Alaska and the northern Yukon.
Gwitch'in Settlement Region: The Gwich'in land claim region in Canada's Northwest Territories, around the Peel and Mackenzie rivers.
Göktürks: The Göktürks were the first steppe empire to call itself Turk. The Orkhon inscriptions are the oldest known Turkic writing.
Günün a atük (Günün a küna): The Günuna Küne (northern Tehuelche) were horse-mounted hunters of the northern Patagonian steppe.
Ha Shuta Enima (Mazateco): The Mazatec of northern Oaxaca are known for whistled speech and mushroom ceremonies.
Habsburg Monarchy: The Habsburg lands were ruled from Vienna and included Austria, Bohemia and, after 1699, Hungary.
Habsburg Netherlands: The Seventeen Provinces of the Low Countries were inherited by the Habsburgs, and their revolt from 1568 created the Dutch Republic.
Hach Winik (Lacandon): The Lacandon Maya of the Chiapas rainforest avoided Spanish rule for centuries.
Hadramaut: Hadramawt is an incense-trading kingdom of south Arabia, with tower cities of mud brick such as Shibam.
Hafsid Caliphate: The Hafsids ruled Tunis from 1229 to 1574, and their ruler took the title of caliph in 1253.
Haida Gwaii: Haida Gwaii is the island homeland of the Haida, famous for great cedar canoes and totem poles.
Hainan: Hainan is a large island off south China, long a frontier of exile for Chinese officials.
Haiti: Haiti was born from the only successful slave revolution in history, declaring independence in 1804.
Halaf and Ubaid cultures: The Halaf culture of northern Mesopotamia made fine painted pottery, before the Ubaid culture spread up from the south.
Halalt: The Halalt are a Coast Salish First Nation near Chemainus on Vancouver Island.
Hallstatt culture: The Hallstatt culture was an early Iron Age culture of central Europe, named after a salt-mining village in Austria.
Halíti: The Halíti (Paresí) are an Arawakan people of the Mato Grosso plateau, Brazil.
Hamburg: Hamburg is a free Hanseatic city on the Elbe and the leading German port.
Hammonassets: The Hammonasset were an Algonquian people of the Connecticut shore.
Han Empire: The Han dynasty ruled China from 202 BC to AD 220. The Chinese still call themselves the Han.
Han Zhao: Han Zhao was a Xiongnu-founded state whose armies sacked Luoyang in 311, beginning the Sixteen Kingdoms era.
Hanis Coos: The Hanis Coos lived on Coos Bay on the Oregon coast.
Hanover: The Electorate of Hanover was ruled by the British kings from 1714 to 1837.
Harakbut: The Harakbut are a people of Madre de Dios in the Peruvian Amazon.
Hariphunchai: Hariphunchai was a Mon kingdom around Lamphun in northern Thailand, absorbed by Lan Na in 1292.
Hatteras: The Hatteras were a Carolina Algonquian people of the Outer Banks.
Hausa States: The Hausa city-states, such as Kano, Katsina and Zaria, were walled trading towns of northern Nigeria.
Havasu Baaja (Havasupai): The Havasupai ("people of the blue-green water") live in a side canyon of the Grand Canyon.
Havasupai: The Havasupai farm Havasu Canyon, beneath its turquoise waterfalls, deep in the Grand Canyon.
Hawaiian chiefdoms: Rival chiefs (aliʻi) ruled each Hawaiian island, under strict kapu laws.
Heiltsuk: The Heiltsuk are a people of Bella Bella on the central British Columbia coast.
Hejaz: The Hejaz is the Red Sea region of Arabia, holding Mecca and Medina.
Helvetic Republic: The Helvetic Republic was the French-imposed Swiss state of 1798–1803.
Henîa-Kamiare: The Comechingón were farmers of the Sierras de Córdoba in Argentina.
Heruli: The Heruli were a Germanic people. Some raided the Black Sea and Aegean in the 200s.
Hesquiaht: The Hesquiaht are a Nuu-chah-nulth people of western Vancouver Island.
Hi Ui (Pame/Chichimeco Jonaz): The Chichimeca Jonaz of Guanajuato are descendants of the Chichimec peoples who fought Spain.
Hia-Ced O'odham: The Hia-Ced O'odham ("sand people") live in the Pinacate desert on the Arizona–Sonora border.
Hiaitsiihi: A small Kawahib group of the Brazilian Amazon.
Highland Mesolithic Hunter-Foragers: Foragers of the Zagros mountains, where goats were first herded around 8000 BC.
Himyarite Kingdom: Himyar ruled Yemen from about 110 BC to AD 525. Its kings adopted Judaism in the 300s.
Hindu Kush hill states: These were small mountain principalities of today's northern Pakistan, such as Gilgit and Chitral.
Hindu Shahis: The Hindu Shahis ruled Kabul and Gandhara until the Ghaznavids drove them out around 1026.
Hindu kingdoms: The source map's catch-all label for Indian kingdoms outside the major empires.
Hindu kingdoms and republics: These were the many kingdoms and oligarchic republics (gana-sanghas) of ancient India.
Hindu states: The Hindu kingdoms of northeast India and Assam.
Hispaniola (Spain): Hispaniola was the first Spanish colony in the Americas, founded in 1493. Its capital, Santo Domingo, dates from 1496.
Hitchiti: The Hitchiti were a Muskogean people of Georgia who joined the Creek Confederacy.
Hittites: The Hittite Empire ruled from Hattusa in central Anatolia. Their peace treaty with Egypt in 1259 BC is the oldest known surviving one.
Hixkaryana: The Hixkaryana are a Carib people of the Nhamundá River, Brazil.
Ho-de-no-sau-nee-ga (Haudenosaunee): The Haudenosaunee are a league of five Iroquoian nations (six from 1722), with a constitution, the Great Law of Peace.
Hohenzollern: The Hohenzollern principalities were small Swabian lands of the Catholic branch of the Prussian royal family.
Hohokam: The Hohokam were canal-irrigating farmers of the Sonoran Desert whose culture faded around 1450. The O'odham regard them as ancestors.
Hokuzan: Hokuzan was the northern of Okinawa's three kingdoms, conquered by Chūzan in 1416.
Holikachuk: The Holikachuk are a Dene people of the Innoko River in Alaska.
Holstein: Holstein was a German duchy ruled by the Danish king, a source of 1800s wars.
Holy Roman Empire: The Holy Roman Empire was a federation of hundreds of German, Bohemian and Italian states under an elected emperor, from 962 to 1806.
Homalco: The Homalco are a Coast Salish people of Bute Inlet in British Columbia.
Homo erectus: Homo erectus was the first human species to leave Africa, almost two million years ago.
Homo heidelbergensis: Homo heidelbergensis was an archaic human species of Africa and Europe, often seen as the common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans.
Homo sapiens: Our own species had evolved in Africa by about 300,000 years ago. Most of its dispersal out of Africa came later, around 70,000–50,000 years ago.
Honduras: Honduras became independent in 1821 and in the 1900s was the original "banana republic".
Hong Kong: Hong Kong was a British colony from 1841, taken in the First Opium War, and returned to China in 1997.
Hoocąk (Ho-Chunk): The Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) are a Siouan people of Wisconsin.
Hoopa: The Hupa are an Athabaskan people of the Hoopa Valley on the Trinity River, California.
Hoopa (Reservation): The Hoopa Valley Reservation is the largest reservation in California.
Hopewell Culture: The Hopewell culture built great geometric earthworks and traded obsidian, copper and shells across North America.
Hopi: The Hopi of the Arizona mesas have lived in Old Oraibi since about 1100, one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in North America.
Hopie: The Hopi villages on the Arizona mesas, centred on Oraibi.
Hopitutskwa: Hopitutskwa is the Hopi homeland around Black Mesa.
Hoti: The Hoti are a small forest people of the Venezuelan Guiana highlands.
Houma: The Houma are a Muskogean people of the Louisiana bayous.
Hualapai: The Hualapai are a Yuman people of the Grand Canyon's south rim.
Huancas: The Huanca (Wanka) of the Mantaro valley allied with the Spanish against the Inca.
Huari Empire: The Wari Empire ruled the Peruvian highlands from about 600 to 1000, with roads and administrative centres later used by the Inca.
Huarpe: The Huarpe were irrigation farmers of the Cuyo region around Mendoza, Argentina.
Huasteco/Teenek: The Huastec (Teenek) are a Maya-speaking people separated from other Maya in northern Veracruz.
Huaylas: The Huaylas are an Andean people of the Callejón de Huaylas valley in Peru.
Huetar: The Huetar were Chibchan chiefdoms of Costa Rica's central valley.
Hul Kuhk’u: A Yokuts or Chumash community territory in south-central California.
Hul'qumi'num Treaty Group: The Hul'qumi'num Treaty Group is a group of Coast Salish nations of eastern Vancouver Island.
Hungary: The Magyars settled the Carpathian Basin in 895. Stephen I was crowned king in 1000.
Huni Kuin: The Huni Kuin (Kaxinawá) are a Panoan people of the Brazil–Peru border.
Hunkpapa: The Hunkpapa are a Lakota band, the people of Sitting Bull.
Hunnic Empire: The Huns swept into Europe around 370. Under Attila (434–453) they extorted gold from Rome.
Huns: The Caucasian Huns were a Hunnic successor group in Dagestan, later subjects of the Khazars.
Hunters-gatherers: Hunter-gatherers lived across sub-Saharan Africa before farming spread there.
Hupacasath: The Hupacasath are a Nuu-chah-nulth people of Port Alberni, Vancouver Island.
Hupd'äh: The Hupd'äh are Nadahup forest hunters of the Rio Negro region, Brazil and Colombia.
Huron: The Huron (Wendat) were Iroquoian farmers of Georgian Bay, allied with New France. The Iroquois dispersed them in 1649.
Hurrian Kingdoms: The Hurrians were a people of northern Mesopotamia and eastern Anatolia who founded the kingdom of Mitanni.
Hurrians: The Hurrians spoke a language related only to Urartian. Their kingdom of Mitanni was a great power around 1500 BC.
Huu-ay-aht: The Huu-ay-aht are a Nuu-chah-nulth people of Barkley Sound on Vancouver Island.
Hyderabad State: Hyderabad was the largest princely state in India, ruled by the Nizams from 1724 until India annexed it in 1948.
Hän: The Hän are a Dene people of the upper Yukon River, around Dawson City and Eagle.
Hñähñu (Otomí): The Otomí are an Otomanguean people of central Mexico. They are among the region's oldest inhabitants.
Hövsgöl Nuur: The Lake Khövsgöl region of northern Mongolia, home to reindeer herders.
I'târap: A small Indigenous community of Rondônia, Brazil.
Ibadan: Ibadan was a Yoruba war-camp that became a city-state and the strongest Yoruba power of the 1800s.
Ibadites: The Ibadis, followers of a moderate branch of Islam, lived in Saharan oases such as the M'zab valley.
Iceland: Iceland was a Danish dependency until 1918, independent under the Danish king until 1944, and then a republic.
Icelandic Commonwealth: The Icelandic Commonwealth was a chieftain republic from 930 with no king, governed by the Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments.
Idrisid dynasty: The Idrisids, descendants of the Prophet, founded Morocco's first Islamic dynasty in 788 and built Fez.
Ifat: Ifat was a Muslim sultanate of the Ethiopian highlands' eastern edge, a rival of the Christian kingdom.
Ijku (Arhuaco): The Arhuaco are a Chibchan people of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia.
Ikitu: The Iquito are a small Zaparoan people of the Peruvian Amazon.
Ikolen: The Ikolen (Gavião) are a Tupi–Mondé people of Rondônia, Brazil.
Ikoots/Kunajts/Ikoojts (Huave): The Ikoots (Huave) are lagoon fishers of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca.
Ikpeng: The Ikpeng are a Carib-speaking people of the Xingu Indigenous Park, Brazil.
Ilkhanate: The Ilkhanate was the Mongol khanate of Persia founded by Hülegü, who sacked Baghdad in 1258.
Illinois: The Illinois Confederation were Algonquian peoples of the upper Mississippi, allied with the French.
Illyrians: The Illyrians were Indo-European peoples of the western Balkans, known to Greeks and Romans as pirates and warriors.
Imbangala: The Imbangala were a warrior society of Angola who founded the slave-trading state of Kasanje.
Imerina: Imerina was the highland Merina kingdom of Madagascar, which united most of the island in the 1800s.
Imperial Japan: Meiji Japan rapidly industrialised after 1868 and won wars against China (1894–1895) and Russia (1904–1905).
Imperial Japan (Fujiwara): The Heian court at Kyoto was dominated by Fujiwara regents. This was the era of The Tale of Genji.
In-SHUCK-ch: The In-SHUCK-ch are a St'át'imc people of the lower Lillooet River, British Columbia.
Inca Empire: The Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu) was the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas, linked by a 40,000 km road network.
India: India became independent on 15 August 1947 and a republic in 1950.
Indo-Scythians and Yuezhi: Around 100 BC, nomads pushed out of Central Asia, the Sakas and Yuezhi, were taking over Bactria and northwest India.
Indonesia: Indonesia declared independence in 1945 and won Dutch recognition in 1949 after a four-year war.
Indus valley civilization: The Harappan cities, such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, had grid streets, drains and a script that is still undeciphered.
Ineseño: The Ineseño were Chumash people of the Santa Ynez valley in California.
Inga: The Inga are Quechua-speaking people of Colombia's Putumayo, descendants of Inca-era colonists.
Inikana/Kukama Kukamiria/Kokama: The Kukama are a Tupi people of the Peruvian and Brazilian Amazon.
Iningai: The Iningai are Aboriginal people of central-west Queensland.
Inkal Awá: The Awá of the Ecuador–Colombia border forests.
Innu: The Innu are Algonquian caribou hunters of the Labrador–Quebec peninsula.
Inuit: The Inuit, descendants of the Thule people, spread across the Arctic from Alaska to Greenland after about 1000.

Irritilas: The Irritila were lagoon-dwelling hunter-gatherers of La Laguna, Coahuila and Durango.
Irritilas/Lagunero: The Irritila were the "lagoon people" of the Nazas and Aguanaval basins in Mexico.

Iskonawa: The Iskonawa are a tiny Panoan people of the Peruvian Amazon.

Itelmen: The Itelmen are the Indigenous people of Kamchatka, conquered by Russia in the 1700s.

Jordan: The Hashemite kingdom of Transjordan became independent in 1946 and Jordan in 1949.

Judea: Judea was a Roman client kingdom under Herod the Great, who rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem.

Ka'apor: The Ka'apor are a Tupi–Guarani people of Maranhão, Brazil, known for featherwork.

Opelousas: The Opelousa were a people of south-central Louisiana.

Orissa: Orissa (Odisha) was a kingdom of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, which built the Konark Sun Temple.
Oro Win/Oro Towati’: A small Chapakuran people of Rondônia.
Oromo: The Oromo are Cushitic pastoralists who expanded across Ethiopia in the 1500s, organised by the gadaa age-grade system.

Osage (Oklahoma): The Osage Reservation in Oklahoma, scene of the 1920s Osage murders.
Ostrogoths: The Ostrogoths were a Gothic people. Their king Theodoric ruled Italy from 493 to 526.
Otavalo: The Otavalo are a Kichwa people of Ecuador, famous for weaving and trade.

Oto: The Otoe were a Siouan people of the lower Platte River.
Otoe-Missouri (Oklahoma): The Oklahoma lands of the Otoe-Missouria Tribe.
Otomies: The Otomí were a people of central Mexico and Chichimeca frontier allies of Spain.
Ottawa (Oklahoma): The Oklahoma lands of the Ottawa Tribe.

Oyo: The Oyo Empire was the Yoruba cavalry empire of the savanna. It collapsed in the 1830s.
Očhéthi Šakówiŋ: The Očhéthi Šakówiŋ ("Seven Council Fires") are the Dakota, Lakota and Nakota peoples.

Pacahuara: The Pacahuara are a nearly extinct Panoan people of Bolivia.
Pacamoro: A people of the upper Marañón, Peru.
Pacheedaht: The Pacheedaht are a Nuu-chah-nulth people of Port Renfrew, Vancouver Island.
Paekche: Baekje was one of Korea's Three Kingdoms. It passed Buddhism and writing to Japan.
Pagan Kingdom: The Pagan Kingdom was the first Burmese empire. Its kings built over 2,000 temples on the plain of Bagan.
Paipai (Akwa'ala): The Paipai are a Yuman people of northern Baja California.
Pakajaqi: The Pakajaqi (Pacajes) were an Aymara lordship south of Lake Titicaca.
Pakistan: Pakistan was created in 1947. Its eastern wing broke away as Bangladesh in 1971.
Palas: The Pala dynasty of Bengal were great patrons of Buddhism and the university of Nalanda.
Palatinate: The Palatinate was the Rhenish Palatinate, given to Bavaria in 1816.
Paleo-Inuit: The Paleo-Inuit (Dorset and Pre-Dorset) were early Arctic hunters.
Paleo-Koreans: Early Bronze Age peoples of the Korean peninsula.
Paleo-Siberian hunter-gatherers: Hunters, fishers and reindeer herders of northeast Siberia, ancestors of the Chukchi and Koryaks.
Pallava: The Pallavas of Kanchipuram built the shore temples of Mahabalipuram.
Pallava state: The Pallava kingdom of Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu.
Pallavas: The Pallava dynasty built the rock-cut monuments of Mamallapuram in the 600s.
Palouse: The Palouse were a Sahaptin people. The Appaloosa horse is named after them.
Palyku: The Palyku are Aboriginal people of the Pilbara.
Pamlico (Pomouik): The Pamlico were a Carolina Algonquian people.
Pamoari: A small people of the Brazilian Amazon.
Pampas cultures: Guanaco hunters of the Argentine Pampas. After the horse arrived they became formidable raiders.
Pamunkey: The Pamunkey were the core people of the Powhatan paramount chiefdom; Pocahontas was Powhatan's daughter.
Panama: Panama broke away from Colombia in 1903. The US-built canal opened in 1914.
Panará: The Panará are a Gê people of the southern Amazon. Contacted in 1973, they later won back part of their land.
Pancala: Panchala was one of the great Vedic kingdoms of the Ganges plain.
Pandya Kingdom: The Pandyas of Madurai ruled the Tamil south after the Cholas.
Pandya state: The Pandya kingdom of Madurai was famous for pearls.
Pandyas: The Pandyas were one of the three ancient Tamil dynasties, ruling from Madurai.
Pankararu: The Pankararu are an Indigenous community of Pernambuco, Brazil.
Pankará: A small Indigenous community of northeast Brazil.
Panzaleo: The Panzaleo were a people of central Ecuador.
Papago: The Papago (Tohono O'odham) lived in the Sonoran Desert.
Papal States: The Papal States were the lands of central Italy ruled by the popes from 756 until Italian unification took Rome in 1870.
Papua New Guinea: Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia in 1975. It has over 800 languages.
Papuan: The Papuan peoples of New Guinea speak hundreds of languages.

Papuans: The many Papuan societies of New Guinea's coasts and highlands.
Paracas: The Paracas culture of Peru's south coast is famous for embroidered textiles and elongated skulls.
Paraguay: Paraguay became independent in 1811. It lost most of its men in the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870).
Paramaras: The Paramaras of Malwa included King Bhoja, a famous patron of learning, in the 1000s.
Parikwene: The Palikur are an Arawakan people of the Brazil–French Guiana border.
Parkatejê: The Parkatêjê are a Timbira people of Pará, Brazil.
Parma: The Duchy of Parma was ruled by the Farnese and then Bourbon families. After 1815 Napoleon's widow Marie Louise ruled it.
Parthia: The Parni nomads took over the province of Parthia around 247 BC and founded the Arsacid dynasty.
Parthian Empire: The Parthians were horse-archer rivals of Rome who destroyed Crassus's army at Carrhae in 53 BC.
Pascua Yaqui: The Pascua Yaqui are a Yaqui community of Tucson, Arizona.
Pashalik of Timbuktu: After 1591, Moroccan-descended Arma pashas ruled Timbuktu and Gao.
Paspahegh: The Paspahegh were the Powhatan people on whose land Jamestown was built in 1607.
Passamaquoddy: The Passamaquoddy are a Wabanaki people of the Maine–New Brunswick border.
Pasto: The Pasto are a people of southern Colombia and northern Ecuador.
Patagonian shellfish and marine mammal h: Canoe peoples of the Patagonian fjords and Tierra del Fuego, such as the Yaghan.
Patamona/Ingarikó: The Patamona are a Carib people of the Pakaraima Mountains, Guyana.
Patawomeck: The Patawomeck were the people of the Potomac River; the river is named after them.
Pataxó: The Pataxó live on Bahia's Discovery Coast, where Cabral landed in 1500.
Pataxó Hã-Hã-Hãe: The Pataxó Hã-Hã-Hãe are an Indigenous community of southern Bahia.
Patwin: The Patwin are a Wintun people of the southwestern Sacramento valley.
Paugussett: The Paugussett are an Algonquian people of southwest Connecticut.
Pawnee: The Pawnee were Caddoan farmers and bison hunters of the Platte River in Nebraska.
Pawnee (Oklahoma): The Oklahoma lands of the Pawnee Nation, removed from Nebraska in the 1870s.
Pawtucket: The Pawtucket were an Algonquian people of the Merrimack River.

Pechenegs: The Pechenegs were Turkic nomads who killed Prince Sviatoslav of Kiev in 972 and made a drinking cup of his skull.
Pee Dee: The Pee Dee are a Siouan people of the South Carolina Pee Dee River.
Pegu: Pegu (Bago) was the capital of the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy, later the Toungoo capital.
Pemón: The Pemón are a Carib people of the Gran Sabana, home of Angel Falls.
Pennacook: The Pennacook were an Algonquian confederacy of the Merrimack River in New Hampshire.
Penobscot: The Penobscot are a Wabanaki people of Maine's Penobscot River.
Pentucket: A small Algonquian people of the Merrimack River.
Peoria: The Peoria are an Illinois Confederation people; the city is named after them.
Peoria (Oklahoma): The Oklahoma lands of the Peoria Tribe.
Pequawket: The Pequawket were an Abenaki people of the Saco River.
Pequonnock: The Pequannock were an Algonquian people of the Connecticut coast.
Pequot: The Pequot of southeast Connecticut were nearly destroyed by English colonists in the Pequot War of 1636–1638.
Peramangk: The Peramangk are Aboriginal people of the Adelaide Hills.
Pergamon: Pergamon was a Hellenistic kingdom of the Attalids, famous for its library and Great Altar. It was left to Rome in 133 BC.
Pericú: The Pericú were fishers of the Cape region of Baja California, extinct by the 1700s.
Permians: The Permians were Finno-Ugric peoples of the Kama and Vychegda rivers, ancestors of the Komi.
Perquimans: A Carolina Algonquian people of Albemarle Sound.
Persia: Persia was ruled by a long line of dynasties. Under the Qajars (1789–1925) it lost the Caucasus to Russia.
Peru: Peru became independent in 1821–1824. It was Spain's richest viceroyalty, centred on Lima.
Petun: The Petun (Tionontati, "tobacco people") were an Iroquoian people near Georgian Bay.
Pewa: A Puebloan people of the upper Rio Grande.
Philippine islands: The islands held barangay chiefdoms and the sultanates of Sulu and Maguindanao, trading with China and Borneo.
Philippines: The Philippines were a Spanish colony governed from Manila (1571) and then American from 1898. They became independent in 1946.
Phrygians: The Phrygians of central Anatolia had a king, Midas, around 700 BC, remembered in Greek myth.
Picts: The Picts were the people of northern Scotland, known for their carved symbol stones.
Piipaash (Maricopa): The Piipaash are a Yuman people of the Gila River, allied with the Akimel O'odham.
Pijao: The Pijao were warriors of the Tolima mountains who held out against Spain until the campaigns of the 1610s.
Pilagal'ek: The Pilagá are a Guaycuruan people of the Argentine Chaco.
Pima: The Pima (O'odham) were farmers of the Gila and Sonoran rivers.
Pinikura: The Pinikura are Aboriginal people of the Pilbara.
Pinjarup: The Pinjarup are Noongar people of the Pinjarra area. They suffered the 1834 Pinjarra massacre.

Pipa Aha Macav (Mojave): The Mojave are a Yuman people of the Colorado River.

Pisones: A Chichimec people of the Sierra Gorda.
Pissaseck: A Powhatan-area people of the Rappahannock.

Pitta-Pitta: The Pitta Pitta are Aboriginal people of the Boulia area, Queensland.

Plain-Pottery culture: An Iron Age culture of the upper Dnieper and Dvina, linked to early Balts.
Plains Miwok: The Plains Miwok lived in the Sacramento–San Joaquin delta.
Plateau fichers and hunter gatherers: Columbia Plateau peoples who lived on salmon runs, camas roots and game.
Pocomoke: The Pocomoke were a people of Maryland's Eastern Shore.

Podunks: The Podunk were an Algonquian people of the Connecticut River near Hartford.
Point Peninsula: Point Peninsula was a Middle Woodland culture of New York and Ontario.
Pokanoket: The Pokanoket (Wampanoag) were the people of Massasoit, who allied with the Pilgrims in 1621.
Poland: Mieszko I was baptised in 966. Poland was partitioned out of existence in 1795 and restored in 1918.
Poland-Lithuania: Poland and Lithuania were joined by Jogaila's marriage in 1386, and together beat the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410.
Polanes: The Polans were a West Slavic tribe of Greater Poland. Poland is named after them.
Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth: The Commonwealth was a vast elective monarchy with a powerful noble parliament, from 1569 until the partitions of 1772–1795.
Polyanians: The Polans were an East Slavic tribe around Kiev.
Polynesians: Polynesian voyagers settled the Pacific's farthest islands, reaching Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand by about 1300.
Pomerania: Pomerania was a Slavic duchy on the Baltic coast.
Pomeranian culture: The Pomeranian culture was an Iron Age culture of northern Poland, known for face urns.
Pomo: The Pomo are a people of northern California, renowned for feathered baskets. The source map places this label further south.
Ponca: The Ponca are a Siouan people of the Niobrara River. Their chief Standing Bear won the 1879 ruling that a Native American is a person under US law.

Pontremoli: Pontremoli is a small town of the Lunigiana in Tuscany.
Popeloutchom (Amah Mutsun): The Amah Mutsun are an Ohlone people of the Pajaro valley.
Popoluca (mixe-zoque): The Popoluca are Mixe–Zoque speakers of southern Veracruz.

Poquonook: The Poquonock were an Algonquian people of Connecticut.
Porter: The Porter culture was a Middle Woodland culture of the Gulf coast.

Portuguese East Africa: Portuguese East Africa was the colony of Mozambique, built on the coast from Sofala and Mozambique Island.
Portuguese Guinea: Portuguese Guinea was a small West African colony, independent as Guinea-Bissau in 1974.
Potawatomi: The Potawatomi were a people of the southern Great Lakes, allied with New France.
Potawatomi-Shawnee (Oklahoma): The Oklahoma lands shared by the Citizen Potawatomi and Absentee Shawnee.
Poverty point culture: Poverty Point in Louisiana is a set of huge earthen ridges built by hunter-gatherers around 1600 BC.
Powhatan: The Powhatan paramount chiefdom of Virginia met the Jamestown colonists in 1607.
Pratiharas: The late Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj were weakened by Ghaznavid raids.
Predynastic Egypt: Before the pharaohs, Egypt's Naqada culture developed early writing, kingship and trade.

Principality of Kyiv: By 1200 Kiev was one of many Rus' principalities, soon sacked by the Mongols in 1240.

Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal: Vladimir–Suzdal was the northeastern Rus' principality from which Moscow grew.

Proto-Tibetan cultures: Early Iron Age peoples of the Tibetan plateau.

Prussians: The Old Prussians were a Baltic people conquered by the Teutonic Knights in the 1200s. Prussia is named after them.
Pskov: Pskov was a merchant republic of northwest Russia, annexed by Moscow in 1510.
Ptolemaic Kingdom: The Ptolemies ruled Egypt from Alexandria, home of the Great Library. Cleopatra VII was the last.
Pueblos: The Pueblo peoples lived in terraced adobe and stone towns along the Rio Grande and the Arizona mesas.
Puerto Rico: Puerto Rico was Spanish from 1508 and a US territory from 1898. Its people became US citizens in 1917.
Puinave: The Puinave are a people of the Inírida River, Colombia.
Punjab: Punjab, the land of five rivers, was a centre of Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak around 1500.
Punuba: The Bunuba are Aboriginal people of the Fitzroy valley. Jandamarra led their resistance in the 1890s.
Purduna: The Purduna are Aboriginal people of the Pilbara coast.
Purehno: A small people of the northern Brazilian Amazon.
Puri: The Puri are a people of the Paraíba valley in southeast Brazil.
Puruborá: The Puruborá are a small Tupi people of Rondônia.
Puruwá: The Puruhá were a people of central Ecuador around Chimborazo.
Puyallup: The Puyallup are a Coast Salish people of Tacoma, Washington.
Puyanawa: The Puyanawa are a Panoan people of Acre, Brazil.
Pykopcatejê: A small Timbira people of Maranhão.

Pâri (Pawnee): The Pawnee homeland on the Platte and Loup rivers.
P’urhépecha: The P'urhépecha (Tarascan) empire of Michoacán defeated the Aztecs around 1478.
Q'anjob'al: The Q'anjob'al are a Maya people of Huehuetenango.
Q'eqchi': The Q'eqchi' are a large Maya people of the Alta Verapaz.
Q'ero: The Q'ero are a remote Quechua community near Cusco, seen as keepers of Inca traditions.
Qara Khitai: Khitan refugees from the fall of the Liao founded the Qara Khitai (Western Liao) in Central Asia in 1124.
Qataban: Qataban was an incense kingdom of south Arabia with its capital at Timna.
Qatar: Qatar was a pearling shaikhdom under the Al Thani, a British protectorate from 1916, and independent from 1971.
Qayqayt: The Qayqayt are a small Coast Salish nation of New Westminster, British Columbia.
Qhara Qhara: The Qhara Qhara were an Aymara-era confederation of the Bolivian altiplano.
Qin: Qin was the westernmost Warring State. In 221 BC it unified China and gave the country its name.
Qing Empire: The Manchu Qing dynasty ruled China from 1644 to 1912, doubling its territory to include Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang.
Qom: The Qom (Toba) are a Guaycuruan people of the Argentine Chaco.
Quapaw: The Quapaw were a Siouan people of the lower Arkansas River.
Quatsino: The Quatsino are a Kwakwaka'wakw people of northern Vancouver Island.
Quechan (Kwatsáan): The Quechan are a Yuman people of the Colorado River near Yuma.
Quechua: The Quechua of the Andes speak the Inca's language, the most widely spoken Indigenous language of the Americas.
Queensland (UK): Queensland was a British colony from 1859, which joined Australia in 1901.
Queets: The Queets are a Quinault-related people of the Olympic coast.
Quileute: The Quileute are a people of La Push on the Olympic coast, Washington.
Quillacinga: The Quillacinga were a people of Nariño, Colombia.
Quinault: The Quinault are a Salish people of Washington's Olympic coast.
Quinnipiac: The Quinnipiac were an Algonquian people of New Haven, Connecticut.
Quiyoughcohannock: A Powhatan-area people of the James River.
Quuiich (Lower Umpqua): The Lower Umpqua lived on the central Oregon coast.
Quw'utsun: The Cowichan are a Coast Salish people of Vancouver Island, known for Cowichan sweaters.
Qwû'lh-hwai-pûm (Klickitat): The Klickitat homeland north of the Columbia.
Rabih az-Zubayr: Rabih az-Zubayr was a Sudanese slave-raiding warlord who conquered Bornu in 1893. He was killed by the French in 1900.
Rajput Clans and Small States: Rajput clans who ruled western and central India.
Rajput kingdoms: The Rajput kingdoms, such as the Chauhans, Chandelas and Paramaras, divided northern India before the sultans arrived.
Rajputana: Rajputana was the land of Rajput kingdoms such as Mewar and Marwar, today's Rajasthan.
Rajputs: The Rajput princely states of Rajasthan.
Rama: The Rama are a people of Nicaragua's southern Caribbean coast.
Ramaytush: The Ramaytush were the Ohlone people of the San Francisco peninsula.
Rankülche: The Ranquel were a Pampas horse people of Argentina.
Rapa Nui: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) is famous for its moai statues. It was annexed by Chile in 1888.
Rappahannock: The Rappahannock are a people of Virginia's Rappahannock River.
Rarámuri (Tarahumara-Guarijio): The Rarámuri of Chihuahua's Copper Canyon are famous long-distance runners.
Rashtrakuta: The Rashtrakutas ruled the Deccan in the 700s–900s and carved the Kailasa temple at Ellora from solid rock.
Rashtrakuta state: The Rashtrakuta empire of the Deccan, one of the "four great kingdoms" of its age, according to Arab writers.
Rattanakosin Kingdom: The Chakri kings ruled Siam from Bangkok from 1782, and kept it the only Southeast Asian country never colonised.
Rayados (Borrados): The Borrados ("painted ones") were tattooed hunter-gatherers of Tamaulipas.
Raška: Raška was the core of medieval Serbia under the Nemanjić dynasty.
Rembarnga: The Rembarrnga are Aboriginal people of central Arnhem Land.
Republic of China: The Republic of China was founded in 1912. Its president Yuan Shikai tried to make himself emperor in 1915.
Republic of Kraków: The Free City of Kraków was a small republic from 1815, until Austria annexed it in 1846.
Republic of Venice: The Republic of Venice was a maritime republic of doges, ended by Napoleon in 1797.
Republic of the Congo (Léopoldville): The former Belgian Congo became independent in June 1960 and fell into crisis within days.
Republic of the Seven Zenden: The Valais was a Swiss ally republic of seven districts in the upper Rhône valley.
Resighini Rancheria (Yurok): A Yurok reservation at the mouth of the Klamath River.
Resígaro: The Resígaro are a nearly extinct Arawakan people of the Peruvian Amazon.
Rhodesia: Rhodesia was named after Cecil Rhodes and run by his British South Africa Company until 1923.
Rift Valley States: These were Great Lakes kingdoms such as Karagwe, Buhaya and Burundi.
Rikbaktsá: The Rikbaktsá are a people of the Juruena River, Brazil.
Rio De Oro: Río de Oro was the southern part of Spanish Sahara, now Western Sahara.
Roanoke: The Roanoke were a Carolina Algonquian people whose island hosted the "Lost Colony" of 1587.
Roman Empire: Augustus became the first Roman emperor in 27 BC. At its height under Trajan in 117, the empire ringed the Mediterranean.
Roman Republic: Rome expelled its last king around 509 BC. Its Republic conquered the Mediterranean before civil wars made it an empire.
Romania: Romania was formed by uniting Wallachia and Moldavia in 1859. It became independent in 1878 and doubled in size in 1918.
Romano-British kingdoms: These were the British kingdoms of western Britain after Roman rule, the setting of the Arthur legends.
Rome: Rome was a city-state of Latium that by 270 BC ruled all of peninsular Italy.
Rome (Constantius): Constantius Chlorus governed the far west (Gaul and Britain) as junior emperor in Diocletian's tetrarchy.
Rome (Diocletian): Diocletian divided rule of the empire among four emperors (the tetrarchy) and kept the East for himself.
Rome (Galerius): Galerius was junior emperor of the Balkans and later Diocletian's successor in the East.
Rome (Maximian): Maximian was Diocletian's co-emperor, ruling Italy, Africa and Spain.
Rozwi: The Rozwi Empire was a Changamire Shona state that drove the Portuguese from the Zimbabwe plateau in the 1690s.
Ruanda-Urundi: Ruanda-Urundi was a Belgian-run mandate, formerly German. It split into Rwanda and Burundi in 1962.
Ruanruan: The Rouran were a Mongolic khaganate of the steppe, overthrown by their Göktürk vassals in 552.
Rumsen: The Rumsen were the Ohlone people of Monterey.
Runixa Ngiigua (Chocho): The Chocho are a small Otomanguean people of Oaxaca.
Rupert's Land: Rupert's Land was the Hudson Bay drainage basin, granted to the Hudson's Bay Company in 1670 and sold to Canada in 1870.
Rus' Khaganate: The Rus' Khaganate was an early Norse-led Rus' polity of the 800s.
Russia: The Russian Federation became independent from the USSR in 1991. It is the world's largest country.
Russian Empire: Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721. It stretched to Alaska until 1867 and fell in the 1917 revolution.
Rwanda: Rwanda is an old Great Lakes kingdom, ruled by Germany and then Belgium. It suffered the 1994 genocide.
Ryazan: Ryazan was a Rus' principality on the Oka, the first destroyed by Batu's Mongols in 1237.
S'Klallam: The S'Klallam are a Coast Salish people of the Strait of Juan de Fuca.

Saar Protectorate: The Saar was a French-run territory from 1947 that rejoined West Germany in 1957.
Saba: Saba (Sheba) was the incense kingdom of Yemen with the great dam of Marib.
Sabines: The Sabines were an Italic people northeast of Rome.
Sabini: The Sabines were an Italic people of the central Apennines, early neighbours of Rome.
Sabirs: The Sabirs were a Hunnic-related people of the north Caucasus.
Sac and Fox (Oklahoma): The Oklahoma lands of the Sac and Fox Nation.
Sacapultec: The Sakapultek are a small Maya people of Guatemala.
Safavid Empire: The Safavids made Shia Islam Iran's religion. Shah Abbas (1588–1629) built the city of Isfahan.
Saffarids: The Saffarids were a dynasty founded by Ya'qub the coppersmith in Sistan, who carved an empire from Abbasid Iran in the 860s.

Saharan pastoral nomads: Herders of the Sahara as it dried out after the "Green Sahara" period ended around 3500 BC.
Sahtu: The Sahtu Dene of Great Bear Lake.
